argument_map.what_is_at_issue: The opening verse of the Kramasadbhāva establishes who the beings of its text-world are: they fall into two classes — the bodiless (aśarīrāḥ) and those abiding in bodies (śarīrasthāḥ) — and both alike are intent on the worship of Kālī (kālyārādhanatatparāḥ). Its move is to open the text by constituting this community of Kālī-worshippers as the frame out of which the following narrative unfolds. As segmented, the passage is the clean tail of a lacunose verse, so only this three-term characterization is licensed by the passage itself.
argument_steps: Enumeration: the verse presents its subjects as two complementary classes in parallel — aśarīrāḥ, 'the bodiless ones', and śarīrasthāḥ, 'those abiding in bodies' — the pair spanning formless and embodied existence.

Predication: to both classes it ascribes one shared defining disposition, kālyārādhanatatparāḥ, 'intent on the worship of Kālī', thereby asserting that Kālī-worship is the single end that unites bodiless and embodied being alike.

Textual move: as verse 1/1 the passage stands at the head of the text, framing the scene — the beings to whom the teaching pertains, defined by their devotion to Kālī — before the assembly, the homage to the goddess, and the Bhairava–Bhairavī dialogue that follow.

Fidelity bound: the segment contains no finite verb (an implied copula, or a clause continued from the damaged first half of the verse, supplies the predication), so no further argumentative content — no doctrine of liberation, no soteriological claim — is licensed by this passage as given.

open_items.text: Sentence boundary and predicate: the segmented passage has no finite verb, and in the edition (Dyczkowski, Muktabodha MS) verse 1.1 is lacunose ('* * * (?) … kṣyayanti pivanti ca aśarīrāḥ …'), so the three nominatives may stand in apposition to the subject of the damaged clause ('they decay/destroy and drink…') rather than forming a standalone nominal sentence; whether v1 is complete or the tail of a longer clause is unresolved.

Referent of aśarīrāḥ / śarīrasthāḥ: the passage does not say who the bodiless and the embodied are (goddesses of the Krama circle, liberated lineage holders, or the assembled yoginīs/vīras of the pīṭha — cf. the assembly described later at 1.29–31 and 1.40); from this passage alone the referent is underdetermined.

Function of the verse: reading it as an opening frame/maṅgala is inferred from its position (1/1) and the text's subsequent structure; the damaged first half could carry different framing content that would recontextualize the three terms, so this reading needs review against the edition's reconstruction.

argument_map.decision_for_l2: Render v1 as the text's opening frame — a present-tense characterization of its beings as the bodiless and the embodied, both alike intent on Kālī's worship — while explicitly flagging (not silently resolving) that the segment carries no finite verb and is the clean tail of a lacunose verse.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** This is the very opening of the IPVV. The maṅgala (the prostration to Śiva) has been
made; now Abhinavagupta expounds the first kārikā — the *spontaneity* (svācchandya) of the Lord. His
thesis: the Lord is not a bare, featureless light that reveals a world outside itself; he is the
self-aware manifestation, the very being of which is to shine forth as the world and to be aware of
shining. The whole of his doctrine (the svātantryavāda) is here in seed.
argument_steps: **The spontaneity as the self-aware manifestation (lines 200–210):** The blue and the other things, without abandoning their blue-ness, shine forth and are one with the manifestation (prakāśābhedamayāḥ). This is the Lord's spontaneity (svācchandya): being of the nature of consciousness (saṃvidātmaka), he shines forth as the varied knowers-and-knowns, with a body that appears as more than the consciousness-form even though it is not more, and he is aware of (vimṛśati) this. The shining of the not-more as if it were more is the "clear" (svaccha) nature, like a mirror: the mirror reflects the wall, the house, the elephant, the horse, the person, the pot, the potter — all the distinctions of parts and part-holders, support and supported, cause and effect — not being more than itself, yet appearing as if it were. Its not being aware of this (tathāvimarśābhāvād) is its un-spontaneity, its inertia (jaḍatva). But the param-eśvara, shining thus, *is aware* of himself as shining — for the consciousness culminates in the reflexive-awareness (saṃvido vimarśaparyantatvāt). **The time-objection (lines 210–228):** The objection: "then it would always shine so." — The "always" (śaśvat): if "sometimes" were a real, independent time, it might be objected; but there is no such time. "At this time" — the word's meaning is nothing other than the sun's movement (the shining sun). So the question "why does the world shine with the sun's movement?" is like asking "why does not the blue shine as yellow?" And if it did not, the sun's movement would not shine either. On the day of dissolution, that very day would be today, not the present day. So there is nothing un-experiential here. The consciousness's non-excess is seen even in the dream, the construction, and the making of a śāstra — so the fabrication beyond the experience is the un-experiential. Hence: "śaśvat" = the impossibility of time-division; "acchanna" = the non-excess of the own-form; "svaccha" = the possibility of the excess-appearance even in the non-excess; "svacchanda" = the union with the freedom of the reflexive-awareness. **The prostration (lines 228–249):** The vṛtti-word shows the identity-manifestation of these forms in the Lord, the powerful Śiva: śaśvat (un-cut by time), acchanna (not partaking of the other-ness of the own-form in the least), svacchā (bearing the shining of the more), svacchandā (free of the other-rest-dependence, the self-resting spanda). He, Śiva, the param-eśvara, is the param-essence of the supreme-and-lower good (the bliss-juice enjoyment and liberation), who removes the saṃsāric delusion of the a-śiva form — to him the śāstra-kṛt makes the prostration. The prostration is the samāveśa (the entry): the abandoning of the māyā-knower's conceit, the subordination of the "I"-conceit, and the rising of the consciousness-form own-nature. The "namaḥ" is a mere indicator (like the other-nipāta), not the offering of a word-form; by the Gītā-rule, the "namaḥ" heard pleases the Lord. The svāhā and the rest, in the offering, have only the indicated meaning (the increase of the flame, the gift to the deity) — not a bare word-form.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The opening of the IPVV has made the prostration to Śiva. Now Abhinavagupta must
explain what that prostration actually is and means — and who is eligible to make it. The commentary
on the word "kathaṃcit āsādya" (having attained, in some way) opens up: the attaining of the Lord is
the attainment of *dāsya* (the servant-ness), and the servant-ness is the very heart of the eligibility
and the devotion. The whole is framed against the Gītā's account of the four kinds of devotees.
argument_steps: **The right teacher and the prostration's form (lines 600–618):** The right teacher (samyagvyutpādakaḥ śāstrakāraḥ) is he who does not abandon the view; the Buddhists and the rest are its makers-and-haters (this is set out in the Kathāmukhatilaka). The ṭīkā-kāra, seeing an un-precedented form of the prostration, makes the "jaya-namaskāra" and the rest, for the ones who support it (the ādi includes the vandana, the pradhyāna). The form that rests in the two [the Lord and the devotee] must, being conveyed through one of them, culminate in the rest of both: "the jar shines, the jar sees" — the jar, being manifested, manifests [its own manifestation] — this is the object-understanding. The prostration is two-resting. The "jaya/jayasi/jayeti" words, though moving by the param-eśvara's excess, must have the self-subordinating as the support (else the excess fails); the "namaḥ/namāmi/vande" words, though moving by the self-subordinating re-recollection, must rest in the Lord's excess. The two are one thing, two-aspect, made manifest by the word for the whole audience. **The dāsya (servant-ness) and the eligibility (lines 618–646):** "Kathaṃcit" (in some way) says that the dāsya is extremely hard to get — so the more is the self-subordination stated. "Mahāphala" (great-fruit): the Lord's excess is attained, being the servant, in the Lord; the "great-fruit" is the cause of the attainment of all the fortunes (samastasampat) — the word is the pratyabhijñā's distinction and the dāsya's distinction (the Vṛtti: "dāsyalakṣmī" — the lakṣmīs born of the dāsya, all the fortunes, attained from the param-eśvara's grace; else the lakṣmī-word would be meaningless). "Vācāpi vā" (even by speech): by the 'api', also by the body. The prostration and the excess, resting in the mental experience (the mind-awareness) and the word-essence, not in the inert body; so the devotee, offering the undivided mind-speech (the consciousness-power), offers the whole world to the Lord. (The āgama: "and he should offer his own self.") **The Gītā-bhaktas and the good-person (lines 646–900):** The prostration by the word is the upacāra (the metaphor), the mark by which the mind-offering is inferred; not the primary [sense]. The "satyam" (true): the removal of obstacles is indeed attained, but the greater purpose is that of the verse-fragment bound to the prostration. The "adyāpi" (even now): un-brokenly, by the entry into the book, the whole heart is crossed; the offering is in that, not in the self. The "vyākhyātṛ" (the explainer) is honored; in the pratyabhijñā's establishment, the Lord's favor is inferred, preceded by the Lord's favor. The objection: "the eligibility suits the explainer, but how the listeners?" — the listener does not establish the recognition, nor the dāsya, apart; the re-recollection is one. [The four Gītā-bhaktas — the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, the knower — are all eligible, in their gradations, for the dāsya and the recognition.]

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The kārikā says "the own-self alone" (svātmā eva) is the Lord. But what does
"own-self" (svātmā) mean? Does it include everything — the inert things, the void, the whole world? The
objector presses: if the maheśvara is the self of the blue, then he is equally the self of the yellow,
and so how is "this is the blue, this is the yellow" possible — how is the world divided? Abhinavagupta
answers by explaining that "own-self" means the *consciousness* that is the self of all, and that the
division of the world is the division of what appears *within* that consciousness, not a division of the
self itself.
argument_steps: **The "own-self" (svātmā) — what it includes (lines 1200–1236):** The "sva" (own) in "svātmā" attracts a relation; being un-said, it is not restricted — so the whole being-class, inert and conscious, is perceived [as related]. For the conscious, he is the one self, of the nature of consciousness. But for the inert — the separately-cut-off forms — how can they have one self, since separate-natured things cannot have one nature (the contradiction)? The siddhānta's answer: here "svātmā" (the own-self) is the own (sva), the self's own — the non-other-dependent, un-conditioned relation (svasāmānyalakṣaṇa, arthakriyākāritva, the non-other-expecting). For the inert, in their inert-ness, even being/non-being is hard in the self — how much less the blue/yellow/pleasure/pain difference. If what is in itself, were not, what would suffer? If it did the object-action, what then? If it shone, what is its own glory? "It shines for me, for Caitra" — how does that fit? If the perception is that, then what is it to the thing? "By that it shines" — that is a new, un-precedented reason (else the white would make the yellow white). If it is the thing's own, then by that it does not happen elsewhere (like the blue's blue-ness in the yellow) — so the manifestation-form is the knower's own; how, then, in the blue? The identity of the being [with the consciousness] is the pervader; else the blue-would-be-yellow and the rest would be the un-fit, opposed to the rule (dṛśyatā-rūpya-pervader- niyama). The identity's other-ness is opposed; and that is the other-ness. But without the blue's being-manifested there is no own-life; so, by the un-removable manifestation, the identity of the being with the knower's manifestation must be accepted. Hence the blue and the rest are the awareness-forms (bodhātmānaḥ), not another body — so their own-self too is the maheśvara. This is the desired. **The void and the division (lines 1228–1249):** "Let the lump (loṣṭa) and the rest be" — for the lump, clearly manifesting, who disputes its awareness-ness? Even the void (abhāva) — the mere "nothing" — as long as it is so, does not shine; then it is other than being. If it is cognized, then the maheśvara is its own-self too; if it is un-cognized, then it is nothing, so whose self is it? The "cognized" word (budhyamāna-padam) answers the objection "even the blue's non-being has the maheśvara as its self": the acceptance of the being-cognized is the answer — else the objection is without support. The nanu: "if the maheśvara is the blue's self and the yellow's self, how is 'this is the blue, this is the yellow' divided?" Answer: all the known is the body (śarīra) of the consciousness-self — as the body, though known, is "I" by the un-metaphorical support (aham-avaṣṭambha), so the whole world is "I" to the consciousness. The I-ness of the body is not the upacāra (as of a tool, like the blanket), even for the separately- self-conceited. Hence the division is not accepted by us: the consciousness is world-form (viśvarūpā), and the blue-yellow series too. (The Upaniṣadic citation: as the space-of-the-jar and the space-of-the-cloth are the one space, so the whole world is the one consciousness.)

Proceed. The argument is understood: "svātmā" is the own-self, the consciousness, which is the self of
all — including the inert and the void (in their being-cognized). The division of blue and yellow is

is "I". The blue and the yellow are the awareness-forms, whose own-self is the maheśvara. This is the
svātmā, and the jñātṛ-kartṛ (the knower-doer) is this one Lord.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** How can the self be the *eternal* knower, if memory reaches only what one has
experienced — and the Rāmāyaṇa was composed by Vālmīki long ago, whom "I" was not? The objection: "I
was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa." Abhinavagupta answers that the *param-essence knower* — the
consciousness-self — is un-cut by all three times; the "I" that was not at that time is only the
present body, not the self. Memory itself, he shows, presupposes the eternal knower.
argument_steps: **The Rāmāyaṇa objection (lines 1800–1816):** If memory reaches only the experienced, then "I was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa" — for that time was not experienced by me. If it is said "from the āgama we know that time," then the āgama too presupposes the experiencer's experience. But Vālmīki was the experiencer then, not "I." The question is apt; but the *aham-vimarśa* (the "I"-recollection) of the consciousness-nature is established as eternal, to this extent. And he is the one param-essence knower; if the other-breaths-minds- eight-fold-city-bodies are distinct, the knower-distinction is made by their difference. So the "this body was not at that time" is the truth here [not "I was not"]. At the dissolution and the beginning of creation, "we were not" — else the special-time-reference would not be. In the "we were not" cognition, the past-time-appearance, brought into the liṭ (perfect) ending, does flash. This is a cognition; and it is not the experience-form (else, like the yogin, the present would flash the past-object). Hence it is memory; and memory presupposes the prior experience. The utprekṣā (conjecture) too presupposes memory or experience at the root. But the pure consciousness-mere, being free of the time-tint and incapable of appearing as a thing beyond its own form, cannot [alone] bear the memory — so the memory is [of] the body-and-the-rest-tinted. The prior-body-tint is distinct from this-body- tint; so the memory-ness is not clear, like the young man who was not a child (the "not-yet-child" state). **The eternal knower (lines 1822–1849):** Where the conceit of the experiencer is firm in the body, there the memory-ness is clear. Enough: it is established that the self's manifestation is not un-precedented (apūrva). The apūrvatva is by being; the apūrva-prakāśatva by the attainment. The self's non-being-before, nor the experience-of-the- existent — in truth, the being-ness rests in the manifestation, so the being-priority rests in the manifestation's un-precedented-ness — hence the sāmānādhikaraṇya (co-reference) is fit. The "cakāra" is not used. The knower's apūrva-prakāśatva-dealing is not without the prior knower (it needs the memory of the prior time); without it, the being's pervader (the non-dependence on that form) would fail — like the cloth without the clay-lump. So the knower's apūrva-prakāśatva presupposes the eternal knower. But the param-essence knower is never apūrva-prakāśa; and all the knowers are un-divided from him — so in truth there is no apūrva-prakāśatā. (The Gītā 2.12: "for truly I was never not… nor these lords; nor shall we not be" — the self, the param-essence knower, is un-cut by the three times; by its un-dividedness, so are the others.) In the māyā-knower, the apūrva-prakāśatā may be, but it rests in the eternal param-essence knower. The pramāṇa/karaṇa is thus grounded in the eternal knower.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The kārikā declares "the self alone is the Lord." But the objector asks: what is the
*pramāṇa* (valid means) for this? A pramāṇa, it is said, establishes something *un-established* — it
serves the practical dealing (vyavahāra). But the Lord-self is already established; so what does the
pramāṇa do here? Abhinavagupta answers that the pramāṇa here is not to establish a new thing but to
*foreground* what is already present, though hidden — the recognition (pratyabhijñā), which is the
jñāna-kriyā power, the content and the firm conviction of the whole śāstra.
argument_steps: **The coming verses (lines 2400–2412):** "Kalā-raised consciousness-essence, agent-ness-made; the inert-form's void-and-the-rest, manifest as the quality, standing" (3.22) — will be said; and "the primary-ness of the agent-ness and the awareness and the consciousness-self; in the void-and-the-rest, its quality, the knowledge is the entry into that" (3.23). The consciousness-form's non-usage as an instrument elsewhere (in the body-and-the-rest); and the rising of the consciousness-form by sinking into the body-form. This is the prabhāva (the power): by which, in the excellence, the other-natured is made to be done. (Said by the primacy of the para-apara-siddhi.) **The pramāṇa in the established self (lines 2416–2432):** The "siddhasya" (of the established) — by own-form and by knowledge. The objection: "for an established thing, the pramāṇa is the vyavahāra-achievement — so only the pratyabhijñāna is to be established in the Vṛtti." Answer: for the inert objects, even the established, the pramāṇa makes a new attainment of some un-established part — at least the prakhyā/upākhyā (the manifestation and the designation) form of the dealing. But in the self, the Lord, there is nothing un-attained to be established — for the prakhyā and upākhyā too are established. Hence even the mere dealing is not to be established here; rather, what is hidden (upāṃśu-cchanna), standing near, is shown as primary by the heart's coming-together. Let the prakhyā-upākhyā of the self, the Lord-form, not be an instrument in the body-and-the-rest and the blue-and-the-rest, but be seen as primary. In the world, for the inert object, the mere-dealing-means, made here in the ajaḍa, is, by the showing, the same — the "see-see" attention-giving. In this sūtra, the "dṛṣṭe" (seen) — by the karma-grammar, being without karma, is the agent; the "dṛṣṭatva" is the undisputed-established-ness, equal in both. **The pratyabhijñā as the content (lines 2434–2444):** The coming-sūtra-meaning: "the self alone is the Lord, and he is established." The pratyabhijñā — the power manifested as the means-being-achievement — and the firm conviction (dṛḍhaniścaya) made by it — made with the reason, shown to the certainty-end. After the upoddhāta, of the to-be-said śāstra, that pratyabhijñā is the jñāna-kriyā-power form — the content (artha), the to-be-said, established by the jñāna-kriyā two-sections (by the āgama-concordant meanings, by the tattvārthasaṅgraha-determined intentions) — the knowledge and action powers are determined at length. And the firm conviction.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The upoddhāta (the preliminary) has two vimarśas. In this second, Abhinavagupta faces
the opponents who deny the self's lordship. Who are the true opponents? The Cārvāka (materialist)
cannot even frame a refutation (having no means of proof); the Sāṃkhya (the many selfs, or one
self with hidden lordship) is not wholly far. The real pūrvapakṣin is the **Buddhist (Sautrāntika/
Vijñānavādin)**, who denies the self outright. Against him Abhinavagupta must establish: the self is
real (the perception/self-awareness), and it is the Lord (the knowledge-action relation is its
lordship).
argument_steps: **The opponents (lines 3135–3162):** Those who dispute the self's being — how could they attain its lordship? They are the root-opponents. The Cārvāka, lacking a stance of their own, cannot refute the other side (without entering the means-of- proof conventions; entering them, they lose their Cārvāka-ness). So the Sautrāntika (the Buddhist) is the pūrvapakṣin here. Those who accept the self — the many (Sāṃkhya) or the one with hidden lordship — are not wholly far; the self's own-mark and the not-accepted dharma can be brought in. So it is the Buddhist no-self that is the real opponent. The 11 verses (from "nanu svalakṣaṇābhāsaṃ" to "tena kartāpi kalpitaḥ") set out this pūrvapakṣa. **The plan (lines 3153–3170):** Two verses reject the perception-self-holder by the non-perception of the seen (dṛśyānupalabdhi). Three reject the inferred-self-holder, saying the memory/synthesis and the rest are otherwise-established. One says the qualities (the cognitions) being qualities, the quality-holder is established. Thus, the self (dharmin) being rejected, the reason for the knowledge-action-relation (the lordship-dealing) is to be rejected: two verses show the cognition's own form as un-established in the other's view; three show the action-relation is nowhere established (no supporter, refuted). The siddhāntin's view (the self, the reason, the to-be-established as the dealing-object) is briefly echoed by the pūrvapakṣin for refutation. The "ātmaiva tu" — the pūrvapakṣin's own view, in a half-verse, shows the self alone [is the Lord]. The 'tu' shows the siddhāntin's view is to be refuted. The siddhāntin, saying the non-perception is un-established, is answered by the "ahaṃpratyayenāpi" (even by the I-cognition): the self is established even by the "I"-cognition, the ādi including the sense/breath/knowledge-stream. The 'nanu' indicates the objection.

The relation's absence: the relation is not — for the two-resting thing cannot be one (dviṣṭhasyānekatvāt), the established does not expect another (siddhasyānyānapekṣaṇāt), and the dependence (pāratantrya) is unfitting. True — but the non-perception gives the non-being only with the restriction of place and time: "here, now, there is no jar." (The verse: "the non-being-certainty is not of the far-ones.") Hence, to announce the universal (sārvātrika) non-being of the relation, one must state a contradiction grounded in the prameya, producing the impossibility of the opponent's own form: "what you yourself said of its form is contradicted by another form you said" — so, by the establishment of the two-form contradiction, the refuter is successful; and there is no dharmin-etc. objection. Then the common-marker refuter is stated: "what stands simultaneously with the own-form-completion of two — that is not one," like the two jars in the two houses [not one]. argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The siddhānta holds that the cognition is self-cognition (svasaṃvid), and the self
is self-luminous. But two objections arise. First: if the self is self-luminous and not manifest as an
object, how does the *yogin* perceive *another's* cognition clearly (the yogipratyakṣa)? Second: if the
cognition is self-luminous only in its own stream, could it not be manifested by another cognition in
another stream? Abhinavagupta answers both — the yogin's knowledge of another is the yogipratyakṣa (a
direct seeing, by the union with the other), not an inference; and the cognition is self-luminous
throughout, never the object of another. This is the Śaṅkaranandana territory (the memory-error theory).
argument_steps: **The yogin's perception of another (lines 6303–6333):** The objection: "if the self is not directly manifest as another's, how does the knowledge of another's cognition shine clearly — since the other-self is not perceived, and the inference does not give the clear-form?" Answer: this is the yogipratyakṣa (the yogin's perception), not an inference. By the rule (yo. sū. 3.20: "of another's cognition, the knowledge, from the saṃyama"), by the power of dhāraṇā-dhyāna-samādhi, when the yogin meditates the non-difference with the other, that meditation, following the thing, and in truth the unity, the difference-conceit being māyā-made, the other's cognition shines clearly — not inferred. The objection "let it be by inference then" — no: the yogipratyakṣa is known. The "paraprakāśyatva" (the being-manifested-by-another) of the self is to be removed. In the yogipratyakṣa, the rāga-and-the-rest (the passions) are manifested; but with their experience, the yogin's unity [is attained], so the experience shines as self-luminous, not as an object. The 'eva' is used after the compound, not "the knower-manifestation" here (the abheda-bhāvanā cannot establish what is always shining). So the other's cognition is a sākṣātkāra (a direct seeing), not a mere inference-determination. Hence the other knower too has no being-manifested-by-another. The Buddhist's other-mind-establishment is refuted at length in the vāsanāprabodha-sūtra. **The dṛk as self-luminous (lines 6338–6344):** The "dṛk svābhāsaiva" (the seeing is self-manifest alone) is the present prameya, established by another route. argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The siddhānta holds that the cognition is self-luminous and the self is one. The
Buddhist's last resort is the *determination* (adhyavasāya) — the act by which the cognition is taken
to establish an external thing. Abhinavagupta now shows that the determination cannot do this: it is
itself only the manifestation-form in the self, and the "external" it seems to posit is not
established by it. And the memory-cognition is not separate from the cognition — both are the
self-luminous awareness.
argument_steps: **The external and the determination (lines 6900–6932):** The external-object-made (bāhyārthakṛta) is only by the strength of the firm-practice-impression (dṛḍhābhyāsavāsanāmahimnā); from the very first, the appearance, shining in the consciousness and in the determination, is drawn-to-the-external only for the slow-minded (in the illusion, the timira, and the rest) — so the error-ness is said from the very first. But he who knows the timira-and-the-rest as the cause of the kakṣā-and-the-rest appearance does not determine the external-ness. So the child who, astonished, cries "the trees on the far bank rush against the current!" is told: "it is not so — the trees do not rush; it is only seen so." This says: the manifestation-dharma alone is this. So, by the non-construction (nirvikalpaka) accepting the external-ness, the error-ness is tolerable in the self; but in the shell-silver error, since the first non-construction does not accept the silver, it is not tolerable — the other-intent. The determination's "third part" (the adhyavasāyāṃśa), in the world-famous error (the "even of others, in the hair-and-the-rest, the erroneous outward-facing cognition" of Nareśvaraviveka), shows the error-form in every determination. So the external, which was to be established by the error-form determination, has no standing in that part — for its inertness. And in the part where there is the non-inert, the non-external, there the establishment is not to be made (the memory-cognition is so). Hence the determination's object-establishing-ness is not fit, like the present memory-cognition. The memory is the upalakṣaṇa. The part that is not erroneous — the non-construction self-experience — does not establish the object (it shines only its own form and self-appearance); so it is un-divided from the memory-cognition, not external-natured (jñānād avyatiriktam). **The determination's failure (lines 6934–6944):** The determination, of the construction-operation form, though it seems to have descended from its own part and is begun to be taken as the object-establisher, does not carry through — the "yāvatā" (insofar) indicates the non-carrying of the begun-conception. argument_steps: **The cognitions un-divided from the "I" (lines 7600–7628):** The cognitions are of the manifestation-mere own-form. How, then, do they not take the form of the "I" when they shine beyond the "I"-part? Their excess over the "I"-part — the non-pervasion, the non-eternity — shining as the object's own-form-place-time-following, contracted — that is made by the object-facing upādhi. But if the object were manifestation-natured, even that excess-conception would be uprooted. The "tathāpi" (still): by the "I"-part-un-divided way. The difference of the object, made by the māyā-power, is only a conceit (abhimāna-mātra); the difference, constructed by the freedom (svāchandya), is of the cognitions — and even in the māyā-state, the param-essence manifestation-form "I"-un-divided-ness is un-broken. For the māyā is the Lord's power; it does not cover his own-form (the power does not cover the power-holder). Hence, by the establishment of the present prameya, the other to-be-established (the vyavahāra) also is established — the self-contained consciousness-non-duality (svatantra-cidadvaita). The "antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpaścidvapurjñānādiśaktimān" (the one whose body is consciousness, with the inner-made-infinite-world-form, possessed of the knowledge-and-the-rest powers) — the sūtra-part. The inner-made, the outer-form, though external, by the knower-form-own-self- one-form-ness, un-lost in the least, made by the freedom-power, is accomplished; and the inner, resting in the one-knower-own-ness, made by the manifestation of the outer-form-ness, the infinite (counted as the four/six/sixteen/twenty-four/thirty-six and more) world-form. **The māyā and the anusandhāna (lines 7632–7644):** The "na cet" (if not) — the vṛtti-kṛt had explained it before, "how?" — the two sūtra-parts ("naśyet" and "na cet") are one sentence, by the hetumallīṅga. The objection: "the arising of the memory was said to be the world's standing (janasthiti); here it is to be said, 'if the synthesis were not' — so how is 'consciousness-form' said?" Answer: "the synthesis of all the padārtha-knowledges, mutually, is the consciousness-tattva." By the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya), by the following-ness (anugāmitvena), the synthesis — the one-becoming of even the seemingly-separate cognitions — is the consciousness alone, inward; not anything else. The "dadāti" (gives) is in the karma-kartṛ. The synthesis by itself, like the cloth-thread-fragments. If the synthesis is the mixing, then the mixer is not other than the consciousness-tattva; the kriyā-kartṛ are applied with the non-difference (their unity in the param- essence). Hence: "from the synthesis is the world's standing" — true; but that synthesis, of the one-object-ness-marker, is not possible by another way — so, by the remainder, it is dependent on the consciousness-form alone. The maheśvara's śaktis (knowledge, memory, apoha) are his; the apoha; and the colophon closes Vol 1.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having established knowledge (jñāna), the jñānādhikāra now takes up memory (smṛti)
and the power of removal (apohanaśakti). The prior view (pūrvapakṣa) held that memory is merely the
impression's revival after the experience is gone ("in the destruction of the experience, memory…").
Abhinavagupta's siddhānta: memory is itself a *knowledge* ("true, but the memory-knowledge…"), and the
whole concern — the aham, the self — is established by memory. His thesis: **memory is the Lord's own
power**, the un-broken manifestation that ties the past and the present into the one "I."
argument_steps: **Maṅgala + the 8-verse plan (lines 31–73):** "Bowing to the Lord, the removers of all woe, the nectar-fluid, the un-thwarted-freedom-unfolding-rest, the nectar-handed-crowned…" The order is jñāna, then smṛti, then the apohanaśakti (the removal-power) within the two. The prior view ("in the destruction of the experience, memory") vs. the siddhānta ("true, but the memory-knowledge"). The plan (8 verses): one on memory's establishment; one on memory's power to manifest the experienced object; one on the entry into unity with the experience and its object; one that in memory the experience does not appear separately as object (even the yogin's knowledge of another does not appear as a separate object); one that memory's separation of the cognition is only constructed (kālpanika), not real; one on the construction's identity with experience; one (the last) that the remembered, the memory, and the rememberer — and, by the way, the seen, the seeing, and the seer — rest in the one consciousness-essence.

— the remembered object's apprehension (lines 48–164):** "Since he is the apprehender of the previously-experienced object…" The memory's object appears in the knower (arthau bhātaḥ pramātari). The refutation of the prior view (the memory cannot be the mere impression's revival): the memory is the un-broken manifestation of the experienced object; the experience and its object enter into unity; the experience does not appear separately in memory. **The aham — inward and outward (lines 165–204):** The "I" (aham) shines both inward and outward: as "the blue-seer" it is inward; as "I, thus" it is also outward. The experience is the outward-natured blue-knowledge. By the freedom of the awareness (bodhasvātantryāt), "I would see the blue" — an inner construing precedes the external blue- manifestation. The place and time of the object, tinting the object, enter the knower and the experience; "I saw the blue then" — the three (I, blue, then) appear entered into that. The object-ness of the experience is the manifestation-ness; it is not a real separate thing (the "arthākāra," the object-form, as against the māyā's prostitute-like seduction). The time-dealing (kālavyavahāra) — "the jar stands, will stand, stood" — is the un-brokenness of the manifestation; the experience is the gate; as long as it is not touched by time, there is no time-dealing.

seducing the self into the object-form; kept as Abhinava's image.
The grammatical point (the tṛc/samāsa in "arthaviṣaya") — the kriyā-vṛddhi; kept close to the text.

Lord's power, the un-broken manifestation that brings the experienced object back into the knower. The

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having established that memory is the Lord's un-broken power, Abhinavagupta now
faces two further problems. First: how can the *past* be remembered, since the manifestation has no
touch of time (the memory's "pastness")? Second: how can the *yogin* know another's cognition — the
famous yogipratyakṣa — if the cognition is only self-cognition (svasaṃvitti)? And more fundamentally:
what is the *nature* of cognition, such that memory and the yogin's knowledge are possible? The answer
runs through the nature of the cognition as svasaṃvitti (the own-cognition), which is also
self-luminous and manifests the other.
argument_steps: **Memory's pastness (lines 700–714):** The objection: "the manifestation has no touch of time — how, then, is the past remembered?" Answer: the pastness is the *being-previously-manifested* (pūrvaprakāśitatva). The manifestation is cut (avacchidyate) by the limiting conditions (the upādhis — the place, the "yesterday," the thirst, the companion): "yesterday, thirsty, with that friend, I saw this jar as un-ripe" — the manifestation, contracted by the place and time, is the memory. In the māyā-word there is no memory-dealing; the māyā-word is precisely the contraction of the manifestation by the upādhis. The memory's object is the being-previously-manifested, re-recollected; the cognition of the object cut by the past experience is itself a fresh experience (abhinava eva anubhava). **The yogin's perception (lines 715–739):** The yogin (per the mā. vi. 4.4, "they desire the yoga-unity") is the param-essence knower; his objects, un-cut by time, are all in his own self as "I," or as "I-this." How, then, does one particular appearance arise for him, and with its past-time-specificity? Answer: the time is the appearing/not- appearing order (ābhāsānābhāsātmā krama eva kālaḥ). The body, flashing and not-flashing each moment, gives the endless time-difference. For those who take the body as the knower — bound by the time-chain — there is no fitness to see past/future. But when the yogin, by the teaching and the prasaṃkhyāna, thins the body, he sees [the other's cognition]. **The cognition as svasaṃvitti (lines ~740–1400):** The cognition's own nature is self-cognition alone (svasaṃvinmātrarūpatva) — that which distinguishes it from the inert. The own-form (svabhāva) is that which never deviates, the un-pervasion/over-pervasion- empty marker. The cognition, self-luminous, manifests the other too (parāpi asya saṃvit) — for the inert cannot; only the cognition, in its freedom, manifests both the self and the other. The yoga- cognition of another is the own-cognition of the other, self-luminous, which the yogin, by the purity and the un-opposed spreading of his cognition, comes to know. Hence: the cognition is self-cognition; and by that self-cognition it also manifests the other — so the yogin's knowledge of another, and memory itself, are grounded in the one self-luminous awareness.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Continuing from the yogin's perception (V2-B): how can one cognition be *known by
another* cognition (jñāntaravedyatā)? The objector presses that the cognition of another cannot be a
real object for the yogin, because cognitions are self-luminous — the relation of object-and-holder
(viṣayaviṣayibhāva) does not hold between two cognitions. Abhinavagupta answers by analyzing the nature
of "being-an-object" (viṣayatā/sārūpya) and showing that cognition is never known by another cognition.
This is the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi territory — establishing the conscious knower.
argument_steps: **The yogin's perception of the other (lines 1400–1409):** The other's cognition, being self-luminous, shines of itself; the yogin's cognition, by the excess of purity and its un-opposed spreading, knows it without the other's self-ness being hidden. But the objector: "even this is established in our view, but not the cognition's being-known-by-another- cognition." **The sārūpya — what "being an object" means (lines 1409–1416):** The relation of object-and-holder does not hold between two cognitions. For the "object-ness" (viṣayatā) of a cognition is this: the *assimilation of the object's form* (tadākārānukāritva = sārūpya). The awareness, taking on the object's form, takes that form as its support (ālambana) — the object's being-alambana is by the sārūpya. And this sārūpya requires both difference and non-difference (bhedābhedābhyāṃ vyāpta): in total difference, or total non-difference, it would not hold (like the bamboo and the pillar, or the jar with itself). But the cognition has no difference from another cognition — the difference of place/time/form is absent, the object-upādhi difference is un-param-essence, and though the object-part (the blue) or the intent-part (the passion) can be an object by the separate manifestation, the *awareness-part* (bodhāṃśa) cannot be an object at all. **The two-mirror point (lines 1416–1428):** Two mirrors can have the mutual-reflection sārūpya, because all their forms (place/time-natured) are distinct; but not so two cognitions. Hence the argument: there is no object-holder relation between two cognitions, because there is no perception of a param-essence difference (vyāpakānupalabdhi). The sārūpya is pervaded by difference; so the object-ness is not established. (Dharmakīrti did not pursue the vyāpaka-vyāpaka considerations — the cause/cause-etc. non-perception is enough.) **The māyā and the awareness (lines 1428–1439):** The "two cognitions" is in the māyā-word. But māyā does not really cover the awareness's own-form (as the burning-power of the fire is not covered); the covering too is, in truth, the producing of a form distinct from the prior state. The objection: "then the cognition would be another's form, and so you yourself admit the difference." — No: in such a state of object-ness, culminating in unity, the cognition is not established as known-by-another. For if the own-form is not manifested, and another form is manifested, then the own-form is not made an object. The cognition is self-luminous; it is never the object of another cognition. This is the establishment of the conscious knower (ajaḍa-pramātṛ).

conscious knower. This closes the smṛtiśaktivimarśa and the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having examined memory (smṛti) and the construction (vikalpa), Abhinavagupta now
examines the knowledge-power (jñānaśakti) that both presuppose. The central claim: **the manifestation
(prakāśa) is the very form of the objects** — the objects are not something outside the light that the
light reveals; their being is their being-manifested. Against the Vijñānavādin (Buddhist idealist), who
denies the external object, Abhinavagupta defends a qualified realism — but grounds the object in the
manifestation. The plan (21 verses): one states the thesis; two that manifestation is the object's
form; two answer the Vijñānavādin; one that the external object is not needed; one rejects perception
of an external thing; two on the inference; and so on to the close (the reflexive-awareness as the life
of cognition).
argument_steps: **Maṅgala + the plan (lines 2084–2110):** "Praising the Lord's abode — full, from the un-surpassed awakening, the unfolding-bliss-will, the rising-nectar-beautiful…" The jñānaśakti is examined in 21 verses: the thesis (k1); manifestation as the object's form (k2–3); the Vijñānavādin answered (k4–5); the external object not needed (k6); the rejection of perception of the external (k7); the inference (k8–9); the objects' necessary inherence in the consciousness-self by the re-recollection (k10); the reflexive-awareness as the essence of the manifestation (k11–14); the knowledge-re-recollection as the known (k15–17); the jñāna/jñātṛ division even in the one manifestation (k18); the reflexive-awareness as the life even in the un-constructed (k19–20); the establishment of the jñātṛ-jñāna distinction (k21).

(lines 2112–2121) — the present appearances:** > Of the present-manifesting beings, the manifestation, of the inner-standing-alone, is fitting as > the outer-self (bahirātmanā). The present beings, as they manifest, have their manifestation "as the outer-self" — the inner standing-alone, manifesting as outer. The memory and the construction do not have a common (sarvapramātṛsādhāraṇa) object by difference; even in the perception, the object does not exceed the experience; and in the memory that depends on it, how much less. The 'api' and the 'yāvat' are read as the sūtra's remainder. The sūtra-meaning: by the present-ness, the manifestation of the beings is their being-inner-standing-as-outer.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having shown that the cognition is self-luminous (V2-D), Abhinavagupta now examines
the *inference* of the external object. The Vijñānavādin says: the cognition's inner blue-form is a
reflection (pratibimba), and a reflection requires an external ground (the arpaka) — so the external
object is inferred. But how, since the external object is never perceived (so no pervasion can be
grasped)? Abhinavagupta answers by showing how the inference works (like the sense-organ, inferred
from the perception it causes), and how the sasaṃvāda (the agreement) makes the determination valid —
so the external object, perceived and confirmed, is real.
argument_steps: **The sense-organ analogy (lines 2800–2816):** The objection: "then, like the sense-organ, it would be merely a cause." The "kevalam" (merely) answers: the determination (adhyavasāya) "I see" is of the cognition-form-object; it is not established by the mere-cause-ness, for the object is the "this." To show the distinction from the mere-cause inference, "nahi": the senses are the cause of the sense-born cognitions, but the object is not — for the "I see the sense by the cognition" determination does not arise. The sense is the object of the inference alone. Here, the special: "the un-grasped, how determined as seen?" — by the sārūpya: whatever place-time-accompanied own-form-variety of the inner blue, all of it, un-lost, of its arpaka (its ground) — by the sāmānābhihāramelana-rule, the determination arises, of the cognition-form-object, from the sārūpya-made error: "this object-form, un-divided from the cognition, fit for the 'this,' I determine." **The sasaṃvāda (lines 2819–2844):** And this determination, though error-born, is not (like the shell-silver determination in the grasped shell) a bare error; by the thing's bond (arthapratibandhāt), determining the cause-able-to-endow-the- cognition-form, even the error is, by the rule "the relation is the pramā" (bhrāntirapi saṃbandhaḥ pramā), a pramāṇa-operation in the self. (The verse: "in the non-possibility of the object, from the non-being, even in the perception the pramāṇa-ness; of the bond-natured, in its cause-ness, the two are equal.") This pramāṇa-operation, by the seeing-strength, taking the "I see" determination-form, uses the perception as the object's helper (amātya iva paravaśīkṛtaṃ rājānam) — so the external object is perceived (pratyakṣagṛhīta). Then the inference's operation: "with the agreement (sasaṃvāda), the root-cause, the arpaka of the forms, is the object similar to that form" — this much is the inference's operation. If the inference refuted the external (like the sattvahetu refutes the stability), then the external-determination would be rootless, a non-pramāṇa-fruit (like the mirage-water); if it did not determine (like the sattvahetu's momentariness), then the practical dealing would fail. The "natu akṣaṇikatvavat" (not like the non-momentariness) — the distinction. The "indriyopayogena" — the sense is used in this cognition, with the determination-accepted-external-object-ness.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Can one infer *another's* mind (paracitta) from its uttered appearances — e.g. infer
Maitra's intent from his speech or action? The Buddhist (Vijñānavādin) thinks the other-stream can be
inferred. Abhinavagupta shows it cannot: only the *aimed* (samīhita) action is the wish's effect, and
the other-stream, being other, cannot be established by the mere utterance (which could belong to
anything). This leads into kārikā 6 — the appearances alone suffice for dealing, and the external object
(whole or atom) is refuted.
argument_steps: **The candana/agni analogy (lines 3600–3644):** As, when one wishes to infer the fire in the sandalwood, if the sandalwood's fragrance of the smoke is set aside, only the fire in general is established, not the sandalwood-fire: the distinction (the sandalwood-fragrance-ness of the smoke) must be accepted — for without it the desired (the sandalwood-fire) is not established. But the other-stream is not established without the "being-gone-to- the-other" (the paragatatva, the first-person-related distinction) — which cannot be inferred. The "being-gone-to-the-other" is not the non-establishedness-of-the-desired's-cause (the kāraṇa); it is the opposed (the kāraṇa-viruddha-upalabdhi). As the sandalwood-fragrance is not a further distinction of the sandalwood (not resting apart from it), so the specific is that which rests apart from the other. Else the "cow" and the "speckled" would both be specifics (the sāmānya-viśeṣa-dealing would fall; the two would both be specifics, and their co-reference would fail — yet "the cow is the speckled" holds). So the "being-gone-to-the-other" of the appearance, resting apart from the mere utterance, is the opposed. In the present case: the "Maitra utters" — the being-gone-to-the-other, of the maitra-made operation- utterance, in the other-knower (the parasantāna, caitrātma) — is the distinction that cannot be inferred from the mere utterance. As the sandalwood-fire needs the fragrance-perception (the vyāpti-grasping, in the palace), so here — but the other-stream cannot be established, for only the samīhitā (the aimed) is the wish's effect; else even the piśāca-like aimed action in the caitra would be established.

open_items.text: The "sāmānyaviśeṣavyavahāra" (the universal-particular dealing) and the cow/speckled co-reference —
the grammar; preserved.
The "piśācaprāya" (the piśāca-like) example — the aimed action of the other; kept close.

argument_map.decision_for_l2:
Proceed. The argument is understood: the other-stream cannot be inferred from the mere utterance,
because only the aimed action is the wish's effect, and the "being-gone-to-the-other" is not
inferable (like the sandalwood-fragrance — the further distinction). Hence the appearances alone
suffice for dealing (kārikā 6), and the external object — whole or atom — is refuted. Only the ābhāsa
is real.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The Buddhist's external object (whole or atom) has been refuted (V2-F, the
shadow/sun, the avayavin, the paramāṇu). But the objector asks: "you established the external by the
appearance-order-variety as the cause; so how is it un-established now?" Abhinavagupta answers with the
positive īśvarādvaya thesis: the external is not needed, because the Lord manifests the whole
object-mass from within himself, by his will, like a yogin, without any external material cause.
argument_steps: **The avayavin/paramāṇu refutation (lines 4400–4443):** The whole (avayavin) is refuted by the shadow/sun argument: the jar has shadow on one side, sun on the other, the middle covered, the two sides uncovered — so the part-holder body, resting on such contradictory parts, cannot simultaneously bear the shadow and be sun-joined and covered and not-covered. The raktādi (the colored) are marked by the covering: in a variegated thread, one part red, another not-red, another black, another yellow. Hence the real-thing's pervader — the being-free-of- contradictory-dharma-connection — its opposite (the contradictory-dharma-connection) being perceived, the whole's real-ness is negated. The same for the atom (the paramāṇu): the middle atom, with two atoms, would have the sun-contact on one side and not on the other, and the middle's covering by both — but the middle, being part-less, cannot have two sides. argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Is action (kriyā) — and in particular the *Lord's* action — ordered or
sequence-bound (sakrama)? And what is time (kāla) and order (krama) in relation to it?
The whole vimarśa (kārikās 1–9) is announced at the start. Abhinavagupta is now leaving the
knowledge-power (jñānaśakti) and turning to the **action-power (kriyāśakti)**. The thread: just as
consciousness's power to *know* (manifest objects) was established, so now its power to *act* must be.
But there's a paradox: the Lord is said to be beyond time and sequence (akrama), yet the world
manifests *as a sequence* (krama). How can the timeless act in time?
argument_steps: **Maṅgala (lines 61–62):** > I bow to Śiva, who — though free of sequence — manifests manifold sequences; the nectar-bodied one, > enjoying the third part of the fourfold nectar-moment (amṛtakalā). This states the whole thesis in one image: Śiva is *without* order yet *shows* order. The problem is set from the first line. **The plan (lines 64–77):** Having established the form of the knowledge-power, Abhinava now establishes the form of the action-power, in eight verses: one to reject the prior view (kārikā 1), one to distinguish ordered/un-ordered (kārikā 2), three on the *nature* of order (kārikās 3–5), two on the division of the sphere of ordered/un-ordered (kārikās 6–7), and one (kārikā 8) concluding that even after dividing the sphere, both truly rest in the one alone. Then kārikā 9 on the creation-power.

— the action of the one is not ordered; rejected (lines 82–108):** > "Hence, although it was said that the action of the one is not ordered — 'the one' and the rest — > [that] is rejected, by the establishing of that one [as the agent]." **The prior view (pūrvapakṣa) being rejected (lines 87–90):** The Buddhist holds that only momentary cognitions flash forth, in a stream, with no underlying owner (āśraya); memory is just impression; and if cognition is inert (jaḍa) it cannot reveal an object, but if it is conscious (ajaḍa) it has no real temporal distinctions. So "how is the self anything other than this?" **Abhinava's reply (lines 90–108), the heart of the kārikā:** (a) distinct cognitions cannot serve ordinary dealing; (b) memory is not from mere impression; (c) cognition, of the un-contracted consciousness, is its own-power-built contraction by the known-object's tint — this is what "power" and "dharma" mean. **The key image (lines 98–103):** the one can be of many natures without contradiction, *like a mirror* (darpaṇa) that bears many reflections without losing its own oneness. So a thing whose essence is appearance (ābhāsasāra), established as one by unimpeded recognition-perception, can take up seemingly contradictory forms in itself and — without itself being divided — manifest those ordered, distinct appearances. This is the action-support (kriyāśraya). The same reasoning establishes the relation (sambandha) too. So, by establishing the one agent, all the objections about the action-power are answered.

— only the *worldly* action is ordered, from the time-power (lines 115–156):** > "The ordered-ness of the worldly action is from the time-power; it obtains, but not of the eternal > [action] of the Lord, as of the Lord [himself]." **Objection (lines 112–113):** "Sequentiality is what action is; and how could sequence be in the Lord, who is not cut by time?" **Reply:** Consider the raising and lowering of a hand. Its earlier and later moments are ordered. The single action, the cause of the division-and-conjunction [of the hand's positions], is inferred — even if eternal — as ordered *by the force of its ordered effect*. So the *worldly* action, resting in distinctions, is rightly ordered — by the **time-power (kālaśakti)**, which is the Lord's freedom that raises the appearance-distinctions, acting as the cause. But the *Lord's own* action — since he is not cut by time — is itself un-cut-by-time, like the Lord, eternal. **The gist (lines 125–133):** in the manifestation of known-and-knower that underlies worldly knowledge and dealing, the knowledge-power is the capacity; and *there* the reflexive-awareness-power (vimarśaśakti), whose self is freedom in joining and the rest, is in truth the action. Though in reality without sequence, it *appears* ordered, because it takes up the delimited [forms] for the sake of revealing the shadow of the known (vedyacchāyā). The Vṛtti and Vivṛti are clear.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
Abhinavagupta is defending the thesis of kārikā 1 — the cognitions of action, relation, *substance*,
direction, etc. are true (by stability + efficacy). In kārikā 6 he has been showing that the
*conjunction* (samanvaya) of the grammatical adjuncts (kāraka) is the action-reflexive-awareness
object. Now, along the way, he must deal with the *substance* (dravya) cognition, which the Vaiśeṣika
grounds in **number and measure** (saṃkhyā, parimāṇa). So the whole point here is: are number and
measure *real features of things* (as the Vaiśeṣika says) or *relational, conventional phenomena*
(as Abhinava argues)? This is the same bhedābheda / saṃvṛti battle as before, now applied to
quantity.
argument_steps: **Step 0 — the maxim (line 1905):** > "No real entity (sattvabhūto'rthaḥ) is expressed without a number." — i.e. every thing we speak of comes numbered (one, two, …). So number seems to be essential to reality. **Step 1 — number is relational, not a free-standing thing (1907–1911):** In that [numbered statement], the number-*appearance* (saṃkhyābhāsa) of the nominal-meaning takes the subordinate position (upasarjana). For it is the very nature of the case-ending-meaning (vibhaktyartha) to be a *quality* (guṇībhāva) in the nominal-meaning. Hence, with the words "one," "two," etc., what is grasped as primary is the *mutual-cut-appearance* (parasparāvacchedābhāsa) — the appearance of each thing as delimiting/being-delimited-by the others. And by that, the *object-form alone* is the number-with-its-two-folds [the one and the many]. "Number" itself, then, is just *the counting of distinctions* (bhedagaṇanātmikā) — it is not an extra real thing added to the object. **Step 2 — measure (parimāṇa) is likewise relational (1912–1940):** [Abhinava continues:] "And measure, too [is such]": > the atom, the great, the short, the long, and — this is the measure the Kāṇādas (Vaiśeṣikas) are famous for. Take first the short-and-long: > the length, though, would be the measure… — so it [length] fits the definition of "measure" (pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa). Now: "measure" (pramāṇa) is *relative to a delimited other object* (paricchinnavastvantarāpekṣa). It is *the appearance of comparison* (samīkaraṇābhāsa): the famous hand-appearance of twenty-four digits (a cubit), with which one compares — and this is *not* a mere external conjunction (saṃyoga). Hence he says: "measure too, as if by an inner-unity-part, of the to-be-measured cloth, measured by the hand — from the attainment of the conjunction [samanvaya]." The taking up of the measuring-rod (yaṣṭyupādāna) is *for the sake of raising the short/long distinction*. [i.e. measure = the appearance of comparison against a standard, not a real intrinsic magnitude.] **Step 3 — atom-ness and great-ness are NOT part-less-ness (1928–1933):** But what is said — "atom, great"? If atom-ness (aṇutva) were *mere part-less-ness* (abhāgatāmātra), then it would belong to the part-less qualities and actions (guṇakarmādīnāṃ abhāgānām). If, on the other hand, atom-ness were the substance's being-part-less (abhāvatva), then it would belong to space (ākāśa) too. Both fail. So: atom-ness = *the fitness to be delimited from all sides*, by the world-famous very-subtle [thing] — the lightest of the mustard-seed, the pod, the small box, the little box (sarṣapaka-vāṭapiṭikapeṭaka). That alone is atom-ness; the other [extreme] is great-ness (mahattva). [i.e. atom/mahat are relational measures of delimitation, not absolute partless/ parted natures.] **Step 4 — the three measures: parimāṇa, pramāṇa, unmāna (1935–1949):** The verse "the measure, though, from all sides" (parimāṇaṃ tu sarvataḥ) is what grasps this. Then: "the prastha-kudava" — of the to-be-measured sesame-and-the-rest, measured by the wood-cup-like, the measure whose mark is the *comparison-appearance* — not a mere conjunction; that too [is] "as if by an inner-unity-part." And the "unmāna," the name, is marked as the "upward-measure" (ūrdhvamāna = weight). The Kāṇādas say unmāna = heaviness (gurutva) causing the falling-action. But that is not so: in mere heaviness there is no measuring-dealing (mānavyavahāra). Rather, the *famous* heaviness — as by the balance-weights (prativartaka) — and its *comparison* alone is the unmāna (so the grammarians say). Thus "measure-ness" (mānatā) is the *same* in the three [parimāṇa, pramāṇa, unmāna]: the difference is only that the measuring is "extended," "around," or "upward," in measure- form. And this is fit — he says "the māṣaka-rakitikā": of the to-be-measured gold, measured by the balance-weight, the mark is the *heaviness-comparison-appearance*. So measure is used, as if by an inner-unity-part, in the dealing (vyavahāra) of buying and selling (krayavikraya), by the greater-and-lesser (prakarṣāpakarṣa) alone. Two examples are written down, joined by the connection. **Step 5 — separateness too (1950–1951):** Separateness (pṛthaktva), likewise, is preceded by the grasping of distinctions: it is the distinction-appearance whose middle is the un-difference that is internally conjectured (śaṅkyamāna). [And it runs] from the number-delimited "one," "separate," up to the "separate" of the far end.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** What is a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), and what is its result (pramiti /
phala)? The whole vimarśa (17 sūtras) is devoted to the *relation* (sambandha) between the known and
the knower. Abhinava opens it by asking what counts as a pramāṇa and what it produces.
The frame (lines 2062–2086): the relation is of two kinds — (a) the known/known-relation
(jñāpya-jñāpaka), resting in the inert-and-conscious, and (b) the cause/effect relation, resting in
the inert. The first is the māna/neya (measure/measured) relation; all establishment of things depends
on the pramāṇa. So this vimarśa determines the pramāṇa/prameya dealing, in 17 sūtras: two (kārikās 1–2)
on the nature of the pramāṇa and its fruit; ten on the pramāṇa's operation per-appearance (not resting
in the own-marker thing alone); one on erroneous cognition; one on the prameya in the īśvara-view;
three on the pramāṇa/prameya/fruit division and the vyavahāra.
argument_steps: (lines 2094–2095):** > The object, through whose force "this, of-this-form, thus" it stands — that is the pramāṇa; and it, > too, is self-appearance (svābhāsa), a new rise (abhinavodaya).

(lines 2096–2097):** > It, the inner-thus-reflexive-awareness-own (antaḥ-stathā-vimarśātmā), in the place-time-and-the-rest > un-divided — in the one-utterance-object, the cognition (miti) is the un-broken (abādhitā) cognition > of the thing. **The argument (lines 2099–2149):** 1. **What a pramāṇa is, in the world's ordinary sense:** the external object (the blue) and the inner (pleasure), *by whose force* the cognition stands firm within its fixed limit — as "this" (by its own form) and "of-this-form" (by some other qualifying dharma, e.g. eternality). That is the pramāṇa, as commonly said. 2. **But then the discriminator reflects:** the object does not stand by its own power alone — for then the blue would not appear *to me* rather than *to Caitra*. So it stands by *another's* power. 3. **That "other" must be conscious:** if it were inert, it would be like a blind man showing the way to a blind man. So the other is of the nature of consciousness (saṃvidrūpa). 4. **But mere consciousness is not enough:** an un-differentiated consciousness could not set apart blue from yellow. So it is the consciousness *tinted by the blue*, turned toward the blue, shining as the blue — that appearance (ābhāsa) is what establishes the blue. 5. **The appearance is of a *distinct* blue:** if the blue were not distinct from consciousness, then the same consciousness would have to be yellow too (since all is identical with consciousness). So the appearance is the shining of a *distinct* blue; and though in param-essence the blue is not distinct from the great light (prakāśa), the distinction *appears*. 6. **The whole creation is one power:** the arising of this is that *the contraction by the void-and-the-rest upādhis (śūnyādyupādhi-saṅkoca)* of the light (prakāśa) — *that alone, by the one creation-power, is the illumination of knower, pramāṇa, and known* (pramātṛ-pramāṇa-prameya). (Cites siddhapāda: "the one light rises, born of pramāṇa, object and knower.") 7. **The pramāṇa = the appearance, in the finite knower:** in the māyā-knower — contracted by the body-and-the-rest upādhis, with the inner-facing experience — that appearance, made distinct as it were, turned to the external known, *as long as it operates*, is tinted by the place-and-time of the known, changing moment to moment, a new-new rise; but in the *same* one, the one word-said, the same one that spans infinite time, related to the knower, my blue-appearance — that alone is the pramāṇa (since that appearance is operative in producing the cognition). 8. **What is the cognition (pramiti)?** "What, then, is the pramā?" — Answer: *that very appearance, of the nature of awareness (bodhātmā), is the cognition (miti), the fruit of the pramāṇa.* These are not synonyms (paryāya): the pramāṇa is the appearance turned outward, of the nature of light; the fruit is the same appearance turned inward, of the nature of reflexive-awareness (vimarśa), contracted by the tint of the object, in the form of the word. In the one thing, the cause and the fruit are both determined by the discriminator; so too in the blue-light-and-its-reflexive- awareness. (Cites pā. vā. 3.308: "by its force, from its standing…") 9. **Why the fruit is the reflexive-awareness:** the operation (vyāpāra) is indeed the fruit, since the instrument's first object is the operation; and the operation is non-different from the agent or instrument being operated. So in the primary sense, pramāṇa and fruit are *non-different*; the *further* fruit (the purpose, the activity, the attainment) may be other. Hence **the reflexive- awareness (vimarśa) IS the fruit**; and, by its force, the *awareness* (bodha) is the pramāṇa. The reflexive-awareness needs the word (śabda) and rests in the general-form-appearance, unmarked by the place-time-distinction-appearances, as its "life." Even "this" (ayam) says only "what is present, and before." Enough: "Caitra stands here now" — so far as it is within the word's reach, this is the path. But by the force of the speaker's own-perception-like own-marker-ness of the thing, there is resting in the specific. So the pramāṇa's operation is *on the appearance merely* (ābhāsamātre).

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** In V3-C, Abhinava established that the pramāṇa operates *on the appearance alone*
(ābhāsamātre), not on the bare own-marker thing apart from all manifestation. Now the objection
arises: if the pramāṇa seizes only the appearance, how can it ever reach the *single* thing
(svalakṣaṇa) that the world treats as one — the jar, the fire? And how can many appearances belong to
one thing? This is the classic sāmānya/svalakṣaṇa and ekatva/anekatva problem, worked out through
kārikās 3–8.
argument_steps: (lines 3199–3243) — the one thing, established by the synthesizing awareness:** > As the taste, as the wish, as the derivation — the appearance, even of one object established by > the synthesis (anusandhāna), is divided. At first sight the jar is one — but the discriminating mind divides it. Division is threefold: by its own freedom (svātantryeṇa), by the wish (arthitva), by the prior-convention (pūrvaprasiddhyupajīvana). How, then, is the thing one? Because the appearances, shining separately, have a reflexive-awareness (vimarśa) that is the means (pramāṇa) of the light; and this awareness sometimes rests in the appearance (giving the universal-dealing), sometimes, with the primary/secondary, "this, of-this- form" — mixing — its life is the synthesis (anusandhāna). Established by that, even in the one own-marker thing, the appearances divide by taste, freedom, wish, or convention, without transgressing the elder's dealing. The synthesis is what makes the many one.

(lines 3264–3265) — the divisions by shape and the rest:** > With the long, the round, the upright-person, the smoke, the sandalwood, and the rest, the > appearances are divided, un-divided by place-and-time. The jar appears long when the eye is fixed on the upper parts, round, etc. The 'as-the-taste' of the prior sūtra is exemplified by the long/round; the 'as-the-wish' by the upright-person; the 'as-the- derivation' by the smoke/sandalwood (a trained perception, ābhyāsika-pratyakṣa — citing vā. pa. 1.35: the perception of the jewel-and-silver that arises from practice). The point: even one thing shows many appearances, divided by viewpoint, wish, and trained derivation — yet it is un-divided by place-and-time.

(lines 3266–3267) — the same for the being/jar/substance/gold/shining:** > Thus-alone the being, jar, substance, gold, shining-ness, and the rest — the appearance-divisions, > doing divided objects — [are] the word's footing (padaṃ dhvaneḥ). The universal (sāmānya) known by the first verse (the general appearance), and the appearance-divisions of the jar (the specific) — both have their footing in the word. The Vṛtti explains the two (inert examples) and one (conscious). The being-ness, jar-ness, substance-ness, gold-ness, shining-ness are all appearance-divisions of one thing, each doing its own object-action, and each is a footing for a word.

(lines 3392–3426) — the fixed object-action through the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya):** > From the appearance-distinction of the objects, the fixed object-action, again — through the > co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya), of the un-divided by the appearance. When appearances mix, one is primary (pradhāna) and is the common locus (samānam-adhikaraṇam) of the others; the relation to it is the co-reference. The appearance so marked, quickened by the sentence- awareness "this here, now, is the jar," is the cause from which the un-divided (those that have attained one own-marker-ness, not abandoning their difference) do their object-action: one action is the aggregate-form (samudāya), another is fixed, each-by-each, single-natured. In the own-marker-ness, the appearance-mere-form-ness, tinging the same individual, is in truth the universal (sāmānya); in the mere jar-appearance alone, it is the universal-form only by fitness (yogyatā). (The nanu: "how can the one, doing many object-actions, be one?" — answered by the pramāṇa = the appearance-reflexive-awareness, which is not uprooted.) The samādhikaraṇya of "blue" and "blue-lotus" differs utterly from that of "Caitra" and "Maitra."

(lines 3475–3503) — the streams-in-ocean: many, yet one effect:** > As the separate lamp-lights, the streams, in the ocean, — of the un-opposed appearances, the > one-effect (ekakāryā), thus the one-cognition (aikyadhī). Separate lamp-lights do not, of themselves, light up one dwelling; but lights gathered in one house do (the single effect). Streams falling into the ocean, with their many waves, do — as an aggregate — one thing. Likewise the jar, the gold, the red, the great: one single object-action (e.g. the great delight fit for bathing the Śiva-liṅga) — so how could the doer of that be other than one own-marker thing? The object-action-doing (arthakriyākāritā) is the worldly being-ness. And the mixing is only of the un-opposed (not of form-appearance and wind-appearance); the opposition is itself by the niyati-power. The one cognition (aikyadhī), the one reflexive-awareness, is marked by the one object-action.

(lines 3598–3627) — the fire/heat: the un-divided object's own-form is fixed by niyati:** > There, in the un-distinguished fire-and-the-rest, from the effect-cause, the heat-ness; the > this-and-this-word-meaning-ness, and the rest — the self, from the one valid-means (pramāṇa) [is] > the thought. Even granting the perception's per-appearance validity: in the un-divided mere fire-appearance, the heat-appearance is that which needs no other thing (anapekṣa), fixed everywhere and always, by the niyati-power (the un-opposed, un-created relation); whereas the fuel-effect, the smoke-cause — these depend on another object (vastvantarāpekṣa). And the this-and-this-word's-meaning (the denotation) is fixed by convention, by niyati. This own-form (ātmā), of the fire, is known from the *one* valid- means (pratyakṣa) — the one that looks to the niyati's glance. Hence: from the effect-cause and the word, the fire's own-form is established by the one perception. (The nanu: the pramāṇa does not operate per-appearance in dealing, since place-time never deviates — answered by "prācuryena" — and why seek the thing's nature by another way? — for the sake of the effect/cause-parts in the dealing.)

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having established that the pramāṇa operates on the appearance (V3-D), Abhinava now
faces the hardest consequence: if the means seizes only appearances, how do we tell *true* from
*false* — the real jar from the illusory double-moon or the shell-mistaken-for-silver? And since the
many appearances are gathered into one thing by the synthesizing awareness, why isn't *every*
appearance-real (atiprasaṅga)? The answer culminates in the great claim: error is resolved, difference
is resolved, and finally **the knower himself is the ground** — so in the supreme knower no pramāṇa is
needed at all. Kārikās 9–17 move from the per-appearance means → error (bhrānti) → difference/
un-difference → the knower as the sole ground.
argument_steps: (lines 4415–4422) — the many means, one operation:** The logic everywhere is the collective of means (pramāṇasamūhamayī). The objection "then is there just one means?" — no: by the difference of object, there must be a difference of form; the perception that grasps a dharma cannot be the body of the inference from a sign (which is the mere fire-cognition). So the operation is *from the collective*. **Kārikās 10–11 (lines 4429–4459) — far/near; the distinct-manifestation-shadow; the un-broken one-recognition:** > By the far-near-ness of the objects, by the indirect/direct-manifestation-own, by the > outer-inner-ness, by the defects, or otherwise of the manifestor (vyañjaka) — 10 > even of the ones with the distinct-manifestation-shadow, from the primary-manifestation, > the one-recognition (ekapratyavamarśa) — the un-broken one-ness is not barred — 11 If the means seizes only appearances, how can the far thing and the near thing be one? The object seen far-off as whole, seen near as whole-in-detail — the one cognition (vimarśa) "this is the same thing I saw far off" is the primary manifestation; by relying on it, the one-ness of even the distinct-manifestation-shadow beings is un-broken (anivārita). The "shadow" (chāyā) is in the appearing/manifesting, not in the essence of the manifestation, which is reflexive-awareness-may. The distinction true/false is not by the pramāṇa's non-contradiction (pramāṇābādhā) but by the *reflexive-awareness's* non-contradiction (vimarśābādhā).

(lines 4500–4515) — the object-action is innate, fixed by the Lord's will:** > The object-action, even the innate, is not of the objects by the Lord's will; for it is fixed by > that — so of it, from the non-doing, there is no other-ness. The object-action is not the thing's own-form (that was shown); nor is it innate (sahajā, depending on nothing) — it depends on the Lord's will and fixity (īśvarecchā-niyatyapekṣa). So, from the non-doing of that, there can be no other-ness — no unreality, no being-another-thing. The "ullekha" (the designation) is the jar and the rest; even with the absence of the external own-marker's object-action (in the Vṛtti's sense), the things are still what they are. The other-ness (to unreality, or to being-another) would require the non-being or the splitting of the nature — which cannot happen.

(lines 4517–4544) — the shell-silver error; the upādhi-place non-agreement:** > In the silver-unity-recognition even, in the shell there is no silver-standing; from the > non-agreement of the upādhi-place, even in the double-moon, the sky is otherwise. The objection: "if the one-recognition makes things one, why isn't the shell-silver real?" — Because although the shell and the silver are recognized as one, the *silver* that appears in the mind-cognition has no standing (sthiti) as the real silver: it is not the external, real, universally- dealing, saleable silver. For the reflexive-awareness that posits it is *uprooted* (unmūlyamāna) — by the non-agreement (asaṃvāda) of the upādhi-place: this place, the shell, is the upakāraka; the "silver" that flashes here does not agree [with reality], and is uprooted by the stable reflexive-awareness "this form is not silver." The *disagreement* (asaṃvāda) = the cognition whose essence is the correct speech of the manifestation-reflexive-awareness, and its opposite. So in the double-moon too: the region of the sky occupied by the second moon is cognized otherwise — "here there is no second moon" — the uprooting reflexive-awareness arises. So the error is real-error (up-rooted), and the distinction true/false is by the un-uprooted vs. uprooted reflexive-awareness.

(lines 4687–4726) — the qualities divide, the class un-divides; the knower as ground:** > With the qualities, the word and the rest, the difference; with the class and the rest, the > un-divided-ness — the bhāvanā, thus, in the one knower, is established. In the beings that shine with the continued-and-excluded self (anuvṛtti-vyāvṛttātmā), neither the continuation nor the exclusion can be faulted, since there is no param-essence-refuter in any part; both shine by the freedom of the experience (saṃvedanasvātantryāt). The difference (by the qualities, the word) and the un-divided-ness (by the class) are both real, and both rest in the *one knower*, the one who re-cognizes (pratisandhātṛ). The difference, too, is fitting only in the Lord, who is capable of re-cognizing the limit of that difference. So the pramāṇa-marker (pramāṇalakṣaṇa) shows the *pramātṛ-pradhāna* (the primacy of the knower): the knower is the ground.

(lines 4802–4803) — the world-picture on the even wall:** > Of the world-variety-pictured, with the even-wall-surface-comparison — touched by the opposed > being-non-being — in the param-essence-real Lord. The appearance (ābhāsa) is attached to the contracted knower; but in the *param-essence-real Lord*, who is pure manifestation, how is the pramāṇa possible? The world-variety rests in the Lord as a picture rests on an even wall (the even wall, with its painted elevations and hollows, without itself being raised or hollow). So the manifestation of the bhedābheda world rests in the always-shining Lord.

(lines 4804–4836) — the ancient knower needs no pramāṇa:** > In the ancient knower, though, with the always-manifested form — what pramāṇa, or the new > appearance, in the partaking of all the cognitions? For the contracted knower, the new-new appearance is the pramāṇa.
