argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The tṛtīyo vimarśa established the pramāṇa, its fruit, and the primacy of the
knower. Now, in closing, Abhinavagupta asks the practical question: given all this, **how does one
actually attain the Lord** (parameśvaratā)? The answer runs through the fourfold "work" (caturvidha
kṛtya), the Lord's grace (prasāda), initiation (dīkṣā), the vision-yoga (dhyāna), knowledge (jñāna),
and devotion (bhāvanā) — and ends in the *jīvanmukta*, the one liberated while living, who needs no
further rebirth.
argument_steps: **The fourfold work and grace (lines 5000–5016):** A supreme (pārameśvara) work must be accomplished [by the aspirant]; even if impossible in itself, it is assumed as possible. The "effort" (prayatna) is the life of the fourfold work (caturvidha kṛtya). **And only by the Lord's grace (tatprasādād eva)** — when the Lord's self is pleased, with the abandoning of the turbidity of body-and-the-rest conceit — is one able to cross the great ocean of delusion. In the Lord-taught śāstra, established by bhāvanā [devotion], the saṃskāra, the dīkṣādikriyā [initiatory rite], the dhyānayoga [vision-yoga], the yoga, the jñāna [knowledge] — by their all-around capacity — [the aspirant] abandons, leaves, the heya-form [the to-be-abandoned] world — the knower-made world of body, breath, the eight-fold city, the void — the world whose mark is the support/object of enjoyment — the world of the lokas and the beings — and, by the gate of the Lord's grace and the guru's grace, in the dīkṣā and the rest, being graced by the param-Lord, he brings the lordship (aiśvarya) to manifestation in himself. This is the connection. **Initiation is prior (lines 5015–5026):** Here the capacity of all the dīkṣā-and-the-rest is stated: even in this birth, the attainment of the param-Lord — although vision and knowledge are primary, the knowledge is preceded by the dīkṣā. (Cites mā. vi. 4.6: "There is no eligibility for the yoga of Śaṅkara without the dīkṣā; and it is declared twofold, by the distinction of kriyā and jñāna.") **Devotion and the vibhūtis (lines 5023–5027):** But if one, without practicing the dhyānayoga, is assured by the jñāna-dīkṣā [knowledge-initiation] alone — then what? Answer: the **bhāvanā** (devotion/contemplation). Some (the yogins) attain a *share of the vibhūti* — a portion of all-knowing-ness and all-doing-ness, the capacity of the higher-knowledge-instrument, marked by the eight-fold vibhūti (aṇimā and the rest), pertaining to this and that loka. But even with the manifest existence of the higher [vibhūti], there is no loss of the present [goal] — and even by reason this is established ("nahi"). **The prāṇa/ātma and the self-shining (lines 5027–5054):** The ātma-being and the param-ātman are both present together without conflict (paraspara-sannidhāna). No conflict from the prāṇa's ātma-being present with the param-ātman; but a conflict of the self-experiencing self-shining-ness? — No: if the param-ātman is present, then he is of the nature of the self-shining one. But then how is the prāṇa's ātma-being? — By the param-ātman's own free manifestation (svātantryeṇa prathā), whose power it is; the prāṇa, etc., shine as ātma by that prabhāva. The prāṇa and the rest, too, have the touched-by-vedakatā (knower-ness), even in vedyatā (known-ness) — the "one"-grasping. And even non-beings (avastu) are thus; even the non-being is [shown]. The object (prameya) is remembered by the power of the break of experience; but the knower-form, whose essence is the un-broken light, is not remembered (spa. kā. 13: "not thus is remembered-ness the essence of this-and-this"). The established [point]: the Lord-ness is not anything new to be proved in the consciousness-essence; the negation of ātma-ness in the prāṇa and the rest is not new either (prāṇādīnām iti). The cidrūpa [consciousness-form] — this was established at length (1.3.6, the "evam anyonyam" ṭīkā). **The jīvanmukta (lines 5485–5506):** In this much, in every way, there is the utter extinction of the delusion-impression (mohakalā- saṃskāra). And on its extinction, by the dissolving of the body-and-the-rest-I-conceit's restraint, **there is the param-Lord-ness itself** (parameśvarataiva). But by the Lord's will alone, for some, even with hundreds of efforts, the recognition (pratyabhijñāna) does not arise; yet even for him, from the mere entry into the hearing [of the teaching], by the order of the ripening of the impression, there is necessarily the attainment of the own-form. (Cites the āgama: "Unwavering in self-experience, he is called the jīvanmukta; but he who still constructs the essence — at the fall of the body, he goes to Śiva.") Abhinava explains: "like the root-leaves of the old tree of saṃsāra, the sparks of the param-real fire — if the inner-intent is ended, the pure-knowledge-fire blazes." Hence, by this, **nothing new is established in the self** (na apūrvaṃ kiñcit prasādhya te svātmani) — this is what was declared at the beginning of the śāstra (1.1.2: "in the agent, the knower, the own self, the ādi-siddha"). And the colophon: the pramāṇatatphalaprameyaparamārthavimarśaḥ tṛtīyaḥ || 3 || — the close of the tṛtīyo vimarśa.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** In the tṛtīyo vimarśa, the *relation* (sambandha) was shown to be the expansion of
the action-power (kriyāśaktisphāra). Now Abhinava examines the second great relation: **cause and
effect (kāryakāraṇatā)**. His thesis, announced at once: **the essence of cause-and-effect is nothing
but the relation of agent and object of action (kartṛ-karmatva)** — i.e. causality is ultimately the
conscious knower's agency. Against this he must (a) show the inert (jaḍa) has no real causal power,
(b) prove the conscious alone is the agent, (c) handle the anumāna/svabhāvahetu, (d) co-opt the
Buddhist and Sāṃkhya causal theories, and (e) show that even so the knower's agency requires the Lord.
argument_steps: **Maṅgala + the 21-verse plan (lines 5516–5538):** "By the meld of the param-essence-unity, I remember Hara, the great cause of the whole, the three-power-joined form…" The plan: kārikā 1 states the thesis (agent-object-ness is the essence of cause-effect); 3 reject the inert's causality (2–4); 6 prove the conscious alone is the agent (5–10); 3 show the niyati-power must be used in the anumāna (from the consideration of the cause); 3 show the Śākya's (Buddhist) causality rests on our way; 3 show the Kāpila's (Sāṃkhya) too; and 2 show that even the conscious's agency, established, does not carry over to non-lordship — it requires the Lord.

(lines 5540–5564) — the Lord manifests by his will:** > This one, from his infinite-power-ness, thus manifests these beings; by his will — this is his > action, his making-ness. This ancient knower manifests the beings without break. How? By the un-divided, un-ordered will (icchā), which is non-different from the Lord. Where are these beings [for him]? In his infinite power — all beings are his powers (1.5.10). This very will-driven manifesting is the Lord's instrument, his making-ness/creating-ness (nirmātṛtā, sraṣṭṛtā). (Against the objection "if the will is eternal, then creation and destruction would be simultaneous; if occasional, some other cause is needed" — Abhinava answers: the will is tinted by the distinction of the object-to-be, so it is not simultaneous.) **Kārikās 2–4 (lines 5596–5613) — the inert has no causal power (the satkāryavāda):** [Full argument captured in the Ratié mining — the Sāṃkhya/Buddhist satkāryavāda: the inert seed cannot endow the sprout with being; the effect is either existent or non-existent, and the "both/ neither" is self-contradictory; the non-existent cannot acquire existence ("the blue cannot become yellow"); the existent needs no acquisition. Conclusion: causality is not a power of the inert.] **Kārikās 5–10 (lines 5679–5927) — the conscious alone is the agent:**

: thus the one action is she, with-order, inner-outer standing. Kārikā 6: the outer of that alone is the effect, which-inner-with-respect-to-which. Kārikā 7: the own alone is the cause, by that he in the two-appearance-standing. Kārikā 8: thence alone in the sprout-even the wished cause is the param-Lord. Kārikā 9: thus-indeed the potter, he, with-the-Lord-ness-alone-arrangement. Kārikā 10: of the yogins-even, without-clay-seed, with-the-will-power-alone that [effect arises]. [The thread: the effect's cause is ultimately consciousness — the potter creates the pot by his power; the yogin creates without clay; so the inert seed/clay is not the true cause, the conscious is.]

+ the svabhāvahetu (lines 5927–5966) — the own-nature reason:** > The effect, the reason, or the nature — from that alone the origin-root-born. The svabhāvahetu (own-nature reason) has two kinds: the clear-embryonic-cause-effect (sphuṭagarbhita-kāryakāraṇabhāva, e.g. "it is fiery because smoky" — fire is the cause of smoke) and the reverse (viparīta). The second is exemplified by "śiṃśapā → tree": the tree-ness is the cause of the śiṃśapā-ness; the śiṃśapā-ness is non-different from tree-ness, and its presence entails the tree-ness's presence. The śiṃśapā-ness is not a separate thing from the tree-ness; so the "otherness" that a genuine causal relation needs is absent — yet the entailment holds. Hence the svabhāvahetu establishes a real relation (the "cause is necessarily present with the effect"), which is the basis of inference. (The niyati-power: the cause is fixed to the effect; the "śiṃśapā born from its own seed by the ekasāmagrī-adhīna rule" is the śiṃśapā-ness excluding non-tree-ness.)

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** V3-G established that causality is the conscious knower's agency and that inference
rests on the own-nature-reason. Now the Vijñānavādin (Buddhist idealist) objects: "If everything is
appearance (ābhāsa), then cause and effect are just relations *between appearances* — and an
un-manifested fire is nothing. How can the smoke-appearance arise from it, or the fire be inferred
from the smoke?" The rest of the vimarśa defends inference (kārikās 12–16), handles dependence/apekṣā
(15–16), co-opts the Sāṃkhya account (17–18), and closes with the reflection argument for why only
consciousness can bear difference-and-non-difference (19).
argument_steps: **Kārikās 12–13 (lines 6460–6509) — inference across knowers, against the Vijñānavādin:** > From the more, the that-that-knower, the one, the fire-appearance, from this it would be — even > from the indirect, of the Lord, the smoke-appearance, and the rest, the new — 12 > The effect of the non-wandering [reason], the marker, from the other-knower; that-appearance from > that-appearance alone, though, of the Lord, is the other — 13 The Vijñānavādin, holding each stream (santāna) to have its own distinct appearances, took the cause-effect to be only within one's own smoke-and-fire appearances (he cannot sense another stream's appearances). Abhinava replies: in our view, the Lord creates the appearances for all the knowers as one. At the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), the smoke-appearance in the one knower and the fire-appearance are, in the Lord's one creation, the same as in another; so, by the force of perception-and-non-perception, the smoke-appearance arises from the fire-appearance, and the pervasion can be grasped once. And again, for the many knowers (down to the worm and the omniscient), the fire-appearance is *one* (not split by stream); so the smoke-appearance can arise from it, not from another. That fire-appearance, being indirect to the inferer, is the "Lord's-cause" (adhipatipratyaya); it is *new* (nūtana), not like the smoke-born smoke. It is the non-wandering effect-marker, used in the inference, with respect to the niyati-power. The inferer is he whom the Lord has created as one with the other knowers in the common part of the fire-appearance. So the inference across knowers holds.

(line 6579) — "in-this-existing-this-is": the causal relation as the pervasion:** > "In this existing, this is" — the cause-effect relation, which — [is what the pervasion expresses]. **Kārikās 15–16 (lines 6892–6975) — dependence (apekṣā) is not real otherness:** > Not of the own-self-one-resting-ones, the synthesis-missing — even in the being/non-being-word, the > seventh-ending's meaning is constructed — 15 The mutual dependence (anyonyalagnatā) is rejected in the first half; the intent-made dependence, in the second. In all four cases (the cause/effect, either present or absent), dependence is not fitting. The real fire and its heat: the distinction between them is only a constructed one (vaikalpika); the fire, as the shining own-marker, cannot have the touch as a separate own-form — both are of equal cause. So in truth the dependence is one, quickened by the synthesis. Kārikā 16: thence alone the case-ending-meaning, the one-knower-supported. The seventh-ending (locative) is not meaningless nor of a merely constructed referent; it is of the real, supported by the one knower. The "sattāyām" (in being) refers to the external form, not to the second 'vā'-dependent constructed one.

(lines 6976–6980) — mutual nature would collapse difference:** > In the mutual nature of the cause-and-effect two, even — the one-ness alone; for in difference, > there is not at all the mutual own-form-ness. If cause and effect were of each other's nature (mutual svabhāva), then in difference there would be no mutual own-form-ness — the very distinction would collapse. This is rejected by perception; the Sāṃkhya's dry (śuṣka) cause-effect is refuted.

(lines 6982–7015) — the Sāṃkhya's one-substance with order-variety:** > Of the one-self, the distinction, and the action following the time-order — thus there would be > agency, and thus, by the thus-transforming-ness — Even in the Sāṃkhya view (the one substance, e.g. the seed/principle, with its ordered variety of natures — the earlier nature as cause, the later as effect), the *kriyā-kāraka* relation is the first thing manifested: the transformation (pariṇāma), the transition from the earlier nature (given up) to the later nature (newly unfolded), is itself an *action*. So even the "dry" causal relation of the Sāṃkhya is not dry — it already contains the agent/act/object structure, and hence the freedom (svātantrya) of transformation, i.e. agency. The mahat (intellect), the pṛthivīparyanta (down to earth), the aṅkuraparyanta (up to the sprout) — all are states of the one triguṇa substance, and the transformation is the action that runs through them. (The guṇa's varied states — sattva/rajas/tamas — are transformed by the restless rajas into the countless forms.)

(lines 7028–7057) — only consciousness can bear difference-and-non-difference (the reflection):** > And not fitting is this for the inert, from the difference-non-difference-contradiction; from the > appearance-difference, in the one, but in the consciousness-self it fits. The inert is a fixed own-form (pariniṣṭhita-svarūpa); it is a known object, so it is "different" with respect to another (blue as against non-blue), but "non-different" with respect to itself — yet the *very same* nature cannot be both different and non-different (contradiction; the "bhedābheda- vyavasthā utsannā" rule). So the inert, being a known object (like the blue), cannot be many-natured. But the consciousness-self (cidātmā), not fallen into the state of a known object — like the clear, free mirror, or the variegated consciousness (citra-saṃvedana) — bears the appearance-variety as its reflections (pratibimba), which are distinct even in the one. Hence difference-and-non-difference fits only in consciousness, not in the inert. (The nanu: "then why don't the elephant and the mountain conflict with the one-ness?" — because they are only in the mirror: nahi, they are in the mirror itself; the free mirror shows all, even without its own freedom — the mere limpidity is its might.)

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The vimarśa has shown that causality is the conscious knower's agency. Now the
sharpest objection: if consciousness is *one* and the world is mere appearance, how is action
possible at all? For action requires an agent and an object, distinct; but if all is one
consciousness, there is no distinct object for the agent to act upon. Abhinavagupta answers (kārikā
20) that action is the one *re-recollection of the will* (cikīrṣā-parāmarśa) that joins the agent and
object; and (kārikā 21) that this very will (icchā) IS the cause-ness, the agent-ness, and the action.
The vimarśa closes with the ||4|| colophon and the transition to the āgamādhikāra.
argument_steps: (lines 7434–7483) — action needs the one will-recollection:** > Even in the real consciousness-unity, the action would not be, of the appearance-distinct two, > without the one-recollection marked by the will-to-do (cikīrṣā). Even granting that the unity of consciousness is real and that the difference is [only] ignorance (avidyā), action cannot arise — because the jar and the consciousness are, by appearance, distinct two. Without the one re-recollection (parāmarśa), marked by the will-to-do, which joins them, there is no action. The genitive "of the jar" [the agent] and "the object" must be joined by that one re-recollection resting in the other consciousness-essence. So: if the unity of consciousness is real (like the jar's being a jar, naturally established), and the difference is called ignorance, then we must ask — of whom is this ignorance? For the one-form Brahman has no "ignorance" as its absence, nor any separate jīvas, which are only raised by the ignorance. If the ignorance is called "un-explainable" (anirvācya), then "of whom?" we do not know. (The "it shines and is un-explainable" is a yakṣa-speech.) The bheda (difference) is real, for the cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference; and the "bādhā" (refutation) too, being a manifestation, would be difference and so ignorance. This would cut the horns of the hare's head, the sky-flower. If all is from the āgama, then the āgama too is ignorance — a net of illusions. (Cites the coming sūtra "brahmāpīṣṭam avidyayā saha, tato naikāntavādo'pyayam.") The Vṛtti: "akasmāt" (suddenly, no cause found). The ābhāsabheda is the known-side form; the kriyātva (the being-action, which confers agent-ness) does not fit in Brahman. (The nanu: "the inert's agent-ness is seen" — e.g. "in the upper direction is the god-self, the Himalaya king of mountains" — answered: no, the inert has no agent-ness; the agent is the knower; the "devatātma" is metaphorical.) The kāraṇa (the aiśvaryaśakti) is needed; without it, the varied order would not arise, since there is no cause for the occasional.

(lines 7607–7662) — the will IS the cause-ness, agent-ness, action:** > Thus, in this way, with the jar-cloth-and-the-rest-appearance-world-self — of the one who wishes to > stand (tiṣṭhāsoḥ), this very will (icchā) is the cause-ness, the agent-ness, the action. The meaning is clear. And what was said — "it, and, is the action-power (kriyāśakti)" — invites an objection: "In the Lord is the will (icchā), in Sadāśiva the knowledge-power, in Īśvara the action-power" — so how is this division? Answer: the 'ca' (and) indicates the doubt. Not only the world-famous action (of the nature of spanda, movement) but *this* [will] too — the 'api'. The "when- then" (yadā-tadā) are particles indicating cause-and-effect. The action-power in the action is thus explained; the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) — "the will in the action" — is the action-self (śi. dṛ. 1.4: "the three subtle powers dwell in harmony"). By the "thus" (tanmukhena = by the consciousness-dense-agent), the grammarians' view: even in the absence of the other adjuncts, the kriyātattva is seen in the agent; in the absence of the other-adjunct-complement, not seen — so by anvaya-vyatireka, the resting-in-the-agent alone is the action. In "here it does not cook," too, the agents fit for cooking-and-enjoying are manifested as implied by the locus. (The karma's action-entry does not happen without the will — the "uparitar" [the higher]; the upacāra's nimitta is the seeing of the intended specific, placed in the object by the will even as agent.) The "sambandhinī" is supplied (adhyāhāra). The ||4|| colophon closes the vimarśa.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The kriyādhikāra showed that the action-power's form is "the un-clouded manifestation
of all the padārthas" (all the categories). But then — what are these padārthas, the categories, the
tattvas? The jñānādhikāra and kriyādhikāra worked by perception and reasoning. But these cannot grasp
the *whole* — perception is not omniscient, inference lacks the pervasion for everything. Only the
**āgama** (the revealed teaching) — which is the re-recollection of the un-contracted param-eśvara's
manifestation — can measure (pramā) the whole universe. So this new adhikāra, the āgamādhikāra, expounds
the tattvas from the Lord's teaching, aided by reasoning (yukti). Its theme: the Śivatattva is the body
of all the padārthas, and the whole creation is "warp and woof" (otaprota) in it.
argument_steps: **Maṅgala + the authority of the āgama (lines 7666–7716):** "Warp-and-woof having penetrated all, by its own force it makes [all] Śiva-may; he who, rising in the un-surpassed abode, is himself the pouring of nectar — to him I bow." Perception is not the omniscient seer; inference lacks the pervasion for all things. Only the āgama, which is the re-recollection (vimarśa) of the un-contracted manifestation of the param-eśvara, can measure the universe. (Cites spa. kā. 43: "when the will-to-see pervades and stands over all objects, what more need be said — it will reveal itself"; and the rule "the one valid-means is that utterance, true, spoken by the Lord; its word is not refuted by the gross means of men.") So the āgamādhikāra begins. In 11 verses it shows the own-form of the tattvas from Śiva down to the earth, established by the param-eśvara-āgama and aided by reason — the creation is warp-and-woof.

(lines 7719–7766) — the Śivatattva as the body of all:** > Thus the inner-outer operation, the action following the time-order — of the mother alone, the two > un-joined [knowledge and action], the knowledge-action. The cause-effect relation does not rest in the inert, but in the consciousness-form — whose param-essence is manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness; by its freedom it shines as inner-outer, raising the time-order, and, in the knowledge-power's form (as the dharmin, the substrate), it takes on the ordered inner-outer operation as its dharma (the action-power). Hence the jñāna and kriyā, manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness, are un-joined (anyonyam aviyukte); and this is the param-essence form (vapuḥ) of all beings. The Śivatattva, which by the gate of the action-power takes up the whole fivefold work and, being taught for devotion, appears as the appearance-form — is so called. (Cites 1.5.16; the Kiraṇa: "how is Śiva, beyond māyā, manifested as the primary tattva in the mind-ground?" — answered: "the downward-pervasion is of the self-shining Śiva himself" — self-shining = freedom, and the downward-pervasion = creation.) The Vivṛti-kāra answers the "why another adhikāra" doubt: the Śivatattva is the body of all the padārthas; the teaching of it is the beginning of establishing them.

(lines 7954–7988) — the Sadākhya and the Īśvara:** > But from the inner-state-surge, the Sadākhya-category first; in the outer-being-primary-ness, > though, later, the param-Lord's [Īśvara]. The Śivatattva alone is the one real thing, but it has further distinctions. It, by its own power, manifests the variety in itself as by a reflection (pratibimba), and manifests the time/place/order (which is the variety's being action-and-form-divided). So when the *inner*, knowledge-form state surges (āntaradaśodreka), [we have] the Sadākhya — the first category, seen at the start of the teaching of creation, from which the "is, is" (sad, sad) cognition shines, called "Sadāśiva." When the *outer* being, of the action-power form, is primary, then, in the surge of the state, the Īśvara-tattva is to be established after the Sadākhya (fitness of the Lord's impossible-doing-ness). The "tattva" (tat-bhāva = the being of that) is defined (mataṅgāgama 1.5.4: "tattva is that which would be the thing's own-form, manifesting its own dharma; the thing-word, manifest, in the revealed view; which, un-lost from its own course, is extended and come under its own power, extended by no other — this-and- this is the tattva in the tattva-stream"). In the pure-consciousness-group (the mantra-maheśvara), the state-circles, like our inner-organ-known states, un-stained, like a picture just unclosed — that cognition-distinction-universal is the Sadāśiva-tattva; the mantreśvara-form, like the full picture in the external-organ-known, is the Īśvara-tattva. (Cites "in that very Īśvara-tattva dwell the param-eśvaras.") **Kārikās 3–4 — the Sadāvidyā, the co-reference, the known-ground:**

: she, the co-reference, and the true-knowledge of the "I-this"-cognition-two. Kārikā 4: of the this-being-attained-ones, to the known-ground-attaining. [The Sadāvidyā (śuddhavidyā) is the state where "I-this" are co-referent — the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the I and the this; and the categories that attain the known-ground.]

(line 8330) — the āparatva (the un-param-ness):** > Here the un-param-ness of the beings, from the non-self-ness manifestation. [The beings below the pure group are "un-param" (apara) because they manifest as non-self (anātma) — as objects, not as the self. The gradation of the tattvas from the param (pure) to the apara (impure) is the āparatva.]

(line 8378) — the bhedadhī:** > The distinction-cognition alone, in the beings, of the agent-awareness-own even, which — [The distinction-cognition (bhedadhī) — the cognition of difference — belongs even to the awareness of the agent; it is the source of the apara manifestation.]

(line 8421) — the aiśvarya in the animal-being:** > Of that lordship-nature, in the animal-being, the manifesting — [The lordship-nature (aiśvaryasvabhāva), when manifested in the animal (paśu) being, is the manifestation of the Īśvara's nature in the bound state. This sets up the paśu/pati distinction that continues in the vimarśa.]

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having traced the categories from the Śivatattva down through the pure group
(V3-J), Abhinavagupta now descends into the impure realm — the world of the bound knower (paśu). Here
the pure self is covered by the *kañcukas* (the limiting sheaths or "armours"): niyati (fixity),
kāla (time), rāga (attachment), vidyā (limited knowledge), kalā (limited agency). And the categories
of the *known* (prameya) — the twenty-three-fold: the one pradhāna (root-cause), the thirteen organs,
and the ten-fold effect. Kārikās 8–11 give these, closing the prathamo vimarśa of the āgamādhikāra.
argument_steps: — the bheda, the I-ness in the non-self:** > In the distinction, though, one-flavor-manifested, with the I-ness, in the non-self, seen — [The bound state: though the reality is one-flavor, in the distinction the I-ness (ahantā) is seen in the non-self (anātman) — the self wrongly identified with the body and the rest. This is the covering of the pure self by the kañcukas.] **The kañcukas (lines 8822–8851) — niyati and the others:** The relation of cause-and-effect, in the bound state, is a *covering*: in truth the Lord alone shines as "this is the cause of that," yet the *niyati* (the fixative power) is the mark of the limited knower (pramātṛ-dharma): the being-fixed, the being-determined, of the cause-and-effect relation. The seed is the cause of the sprout, not of the pot; the clay of the pot, not of the sprout — this fixing, in the appearance, is the niyati, which in reality belongs to the knower, not to the known (mātrābhāsanadvāreṇa). So too kāla (time), rāga (attachment — the mind-flux rooted in attachment, matsara etc.), and the rest, are the kañcukas that cover the pure self in the bound state.

— the śūnyādi knower:** > Who-and-the-knower, the-emptiness-and-the-rest, in the known-distinct — [The knower of the "emptiness-and-the-rest" (śūnyādi) — the void-thought, breath, body — is the bound knower, who, in the known-distinct (prameya-vyatirekiṇi), is the one who knows the separated objects. This is the māyīya knower.] **Kārikās 10–11 (lines 8944–8954) — the 23-fold known:** > The twenty-three-fold known, which is the effect-instrument-own: of it, the un-divided-form one, > the pradhāna, the root-cause. — 10 > The thirteen-fold, here, the external-inner-instrument-series; and the effect-group, ten-fold, by > the gross/subtle-ness distinction. — 11 The known (prameya) is twenty-three-fold: (a) the one *pradhāna* (the root-cause, un-divided-form, the Sāṃkhya matter), (b) the *thirteen organs* (the five sense-organs, the five action-organs, the inner organ, mind, and the ahaṅkāra/buddhi in the usual Sāṃkhya count), and (c) the *ten-fold effect-group* (the five tanmātras and the five elements, by the gross/subtle distinction). This is briefly stated (the detail is in the Vivṛti). Then Abhinava examines whether the *common-marker* (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) can grasp these (they are not truly sensible); the pradhāna etc. are un-sensible; the karaṇa-tva (instrument-ness) too is not fitting for them. The nanu: "in the un-real (avāstava), [these] —" — answered: their un-sensible-ness.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The prathamo vimarśa gave the categories of the *known* (prameya). Now the dvitīyo
vimarśa examines the *knowers* (pramātṛ) themselves — for the recognition of the Lord in the self is
the heart of the whole śāstra, and to recognize him we must understand the various knowers: the bound
(paśu) in its grades, the pure ones, and the Lord (pati). Central here are the *malas* (the stains that
bind): āṇava (the stain of finitude), māyīya (the stain of māyā, objectivity), and kārma (the stain of
action). Kārikās 1–11 lay out the knower-states, their presiding deities, and the stains.
argument_steps: **Maṅgala + the 20-verse plan (lines 9274–9293):** "Bowing to the nectar-bodied, the full-param-essence of the three powers, who wields the trident, cutting the three nooses (pāśatraya) in diseases and the rest…" Having established the tattva-mass as the known, now the knower-tattva is examined at length (20 verses): one on the Brahmādi-three (k1); two on the division of the to-be-abandoned/to-be-adopted knowers; seven on the stain's form and the knower-variety it makes (k2–8); two on the entry (samāveśa); five on the states (suṣupta etc.); three on their abandon/adopt division.

(lines 9295–9321) — the presiding deities of the knower-states:** > There, in the knower-mere-ness-standing, the Rudra the superior-deity; in the distinct-known-spread, > the Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established. In the state where the knower is pure, with the known withdrawn (upasaṃhṛta-prameya), the presider is the Rudra — the param-Śiva, as the Lord, who by his presiding brings his worshippers to that state. In the māyā-word, the prāṇāpāna-form, he is the third-eyed (unmīlita-tṛtīyanetra). In the spread of the *distinct* known, the presider is Brahmā (in the production of the spread) and Viṣṇu (in the flowing continuation of it). These two, making the "this" primary (as manifestation) and the "I" (the knower- essence) subordinate, are not third-eyed — the deity (daivata) is the presiding-form, and the adhidaivata is the deity-as-superior. The objection "how do the Brahmādi-forms shine with the un-purified form of the Lord?" — answered: as the quality of the intellect (buddhiguṇa), not as the pure consciousness-mere; hence their form is the aiśvarya (the lordship, the freedom as action-power, the knowledge). The duality is explained.

(line ~?) — the māyā-blind, the saṃsāra, the action-bound:** > This knower, the māyā-blind, the saṃsāra-one, the action-bound — [The bound knower (paśu) is blind by māyā, a wanderer in saṃsāra, bound by action (karma). This is the māyīya knower.] **Kārikās 3–4 — the pati and the freedom-loss:** > In the own-member-form beings, the knower is said [to be] the Lord (pati). — 3 > The freedom-loss of the awareness; the freedom-own-even the un-awareness-ness. — 4 [The pati is the knower whose own-members (the beings) are his; the bound one suffers the freedom-loss of the awareness (svātantryahāni) and the un-awareness of his own freedom — the āṇava/māyīya binding.]

— the māyā as the distinct-known-manifestation:** > The distinct-known-manifestation, here alone, the māyā-named, the birth-enjoyment-giving — [Māyā is the manifestation of the distinct known (the objectivity), which gives birth and enjoyment; it is the māyīya stain.] **Kārikās 6–8 — the grades of the knower:** > In the pure-awareness-own-ness even, of-whom-not-the-highest-agent-ness — 6 > In the awareness-and-the-rest-marker-unity-even, of-them-the-mutual-distinct-ness — 7 > The emptiness-and-the-rest-un-awareness-form-ones-though, the agents, the dissolution-un-caliber-ones — 8 [The pure knowers (the vidyeśvara group) who lack the highest agency; the mutual distinct-ness even in the unity of the awareness-marker; and the pralayākala (the "dissolution-un-caliber" — those who have only the āṇava stain, absorbed in the dissolution), whose form is the emptiness-and-the-rest un-awareness.] **Kārikās 9–10 — the kārma stain, the three-fold stain:** > Of the awareness-ones-even agent-ness-possessing, in the action-stain-ness — 9 > Of the gods-and-the-rest, and of all the becoming-ones, the three-fold stain — 10 [Even the aware agents are in the kārma stain; and all the becoming ones (gods, men, etc.) have the three-fold stain: āṇava, māyīya, kārma.]

— the kalā-raised consciousness-essence:** > The time-raised (kalā-udbalita), this, the consciousness-essence, the agent-ness-made — [The kalā (the limited agency) raises the consciousness-essence as the agent-ness; the last of the kañcukas binding the self to limited agency.]

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** Having examined the knowers and the stains, Abhinavagupta now examines the *states*
(avasthā) of the bound knower — jāgrat (waking), svapna (dream), suṣupta (deep sleep), and turya (the
fourth) — and the vital breaths (prāṇādi) that sustain them. The point: these states are the stages in
which the bound soul lives, and understanding them — which are to be adopted (upādeya) and which
abandoned (heya) — is essential to the recognition. The pure fourth state is the goal; the other three
are the round of the bound.
argument_steps: — the primacy of agency, awareness, consciousness-self:** > The primary-ness of the agent-ness, and of the awareness, and of the consciousness-self — [The knower's essence: agency (kartṛtā), awareness (bodha), and the consciousness-self (cidātman) are primary. This frames the whole — the knower is fundamentally the free conscious agent.]

— the emptiness, the I-ness-word:** > In the emptiness, the intellect-and-the-rest-absence-own, the I-ness, the agent-ness-word — [In the state of the void (śūnya), where the intellect and the rest are absent, the "I-ness" and the "agent-ness" are only words — the pralayākala, dissolved in the void, has the mere trace of the "I".]

— the inner operation of the senses, the breath-stimulating:** > The inner operation of the senses, the breath-and-the-rest-stimulating, the thought — [The prāṇa (the vital breath) is the inner operation that stimulates the senses; it is the life of the bound knower, the link between the self and the senses.]

— suṣupta, the sleep like dissolution (lines 10326–10361):** > In the that-much-standing, the said, the sleep-like-the-dissolution-equal — with the known, and > without-the-known, with-the-māyā-stain, and-without — In the mere void (śūnyamātra) — the pure void — when the standing is the I-ness-rest (ahantāviśrānti), and when [it is] in the prāṇa, then the consciousness is put to sleep by the māyā (which makes the stain descend), not even awakened by kalā and vidyā. This is the suṣupta (deep sleep): the pravṛtti-cause-form appearance, and the karma (as the action-form) whose essence is the reflexive-awareness. Deep sleep is like dissolution (pralaya) — but in dissolution there is the long decay of the body; here, in sleep, there is no such action and no long time. Its sub-kinds: sleep (by fatigue), fainting (by shock/dhātu-disease), intoxication/madness (by wine, etc.), samādhi (by the freedom-raised effort). The first half is "with the known" (savedya, the vidyākalā grade, with the māyā-stain), the second "without the known" (apavedya, without the māyā-stain, the pralayākala).

— svapna, the dream (lines 10367–10401):** > In the mind-mere-path even, with the sense-object-ness, from the delusion — the clear-manifestation > creation of the beings, the dream-word, the thought. In the dream, the sense-organs (the eyes and the rest) are fixed, yet one sees the beloved, and the cognition "I see her, I draw her with my hand" is a clear manifestation whose primary [source] is the momentary Lord-creation. Only the mind is active, relying on the prior creation; but in the sense-object-part, [the dream] shares the common [world]; the stability and the rest of the appearance, joined, continue the reflexive-awareness — and in the waking state, this is refuted, so the dream is of the delusion-form. The dream is the mind's own creation, a clear-appearance making.

— jāgrat, the waking (lines 10432–10461):** > With-the-all-sense-object-ness, which-though-with-the-external-ness-firm — the creation, the > common, of-all-the-knowers, that is the waking. The waking state is the *common* creation (sādhāraṇī sṛṣṭi), firm and external, shared by all the knowers. The waking knower is he who, by the exhaustion of the delusion-causing sleep, "wakes" — so the waking is the knower-state. The five states (waking, dream, deep sleep, and the two grades) are the knower-ness made by the difference of the known, as taught in the āgamas; and even in the waking the dream-form is found (the mutual entry of the states).

— the three as removable (lines 10444–10461):** > The removable, the three, this, of the breath-and-the-rest, from the primary-ness, in the > agent-ness-quality — from its decrease-increase-mostly-joined-suffering-pleasure — The three states (waking, dream, deep sleep) are to be abandoned (heya) by the seeker of liberation, since the prāṇa and the rest (the vital breaths) are primary in the agent-ness, and the decrease/ increase of pleasure and pain is their quality. In the agent-ness, where the prāṇa is not made primary, its freedom-share, with the pleasure/pain-objects and the gaining/abandoning-efforts, makes the seeker regard the three states as to-be-abandoned. **Kārikās 19–20 — the prāṇas:** > The breath-out-breath-made, the breath, individually in-the-sleep-waking-two — 19 > The middle-upper-going, the udāna-named, the-fourth-going, the-fire-made — 20 [The prāṇa (the in-breath) and the apāna (the out-breath) run through the waking and the sleep; the udāna is the middle-upper-going breath; the turya (the fourth) is the going beyond — of the fire-form (hutabhuṅmaya). The prāṇas are the life-winds that sustain the states; the turya is the fourth state, beyond the three, which is the goal.] **The ||2||/||3|| colophons:** the close of the āgamādhikāra dvitīyo vimarśa and the āgamādhikāra.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** This is the fourth and final adhikāra of the IPVV — the tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra, the
"collection of the essence of the categories." Having established the self-manifest ātmatattva (the
maheśvara-form, the knowledge-action power) at length, in three adhikāras, Abhinavagupta now collects
the whole into a brief summary (15 verses) for the student's meditation. One verse gives the
pāramārthika svarūpa; nine give the bond (bandha) in the direction of the knower/known; five give the
liberation (mokṣa) which is the recognition (pratyabhijñā). Kārikās 1–8 are the opening: the own-self
as the Lord, the bound grasper, the many person, and the guṇas.
argument_steps: **Maṅgala (lines 10899–10916):** "I bow to him, the nectar-Lord, who, in his un-surpassed own abode, makes the drop-made nectar-juice known, the fully-full-making…" The plan: 15 verses — one on the pāramārthika svarūpa (k1), nine on the bond in the knower/known direction (k2–10), five on the recognition-liberation (k11–15).

(lines 10919–10934) — the own-self alone of all beings is the Lord:** > The own-self alone of all beings, the one alone, the maheśvara — the world-form, "I this," the > un-broken-re-recollection-augmented. The sūtra is introduced after the spread declaration (vitatābhidhāna). The non-repetition: those not wanting the spread are graced by the epitome; those wanting the middle are served. (Cites the muni's rule "the desired, in the world, of the wise, is the summary-and-detail-bearing.") The "beings" word carries the burden: "this whole is the person alone." So the teaching is: the own-self alone of all beings is the one Lord, the world-form, whose re-recollection "I-this" is un-broken. (As the Śivadṛṣṭi: "all beings are Śiva; the self of all beings is Śiva" — not that Śiva-seeing is a mere doctrine, but that the self-flashing dharma in them is Śiva.)

(line ~10950) — the bound grasper in the own-created this-part:** > There, in the own-created this-being-part, with the intellect-and-the-rest grasper-own, the > I-construction-re-recollection-word is brought, with this, that. In the own-self, in the mahā-īśvara, in the own-self-mirror, by the freedom, that which is created — the this-part, preceded by contraction; in its middle, the intellect/breath/body form, known by the this-ness; of the that-distinct-known, the grasper-ness-fit, with the I-being, the re-recollection shines. He, thus-form, "I am happy, and the rest," is the grasper, the bound. His liberation is the recognition.

(lines 11028) — the many person, the own-form-un-cognition:** > He, the own-form-un-cognition-made, the many person, is the thought; there in the creation, the > action-bliss two, the enjoyment, is the suffering-pleasure-own. Truly, no one is bound; in truth the one free Śiva is consciousness-natured. But when the contracted consciousness manifests, then the un-cognition of the own complete form — with the longing for the full bliss, the to-be-abandoned-appearance, the woven warp-and-woof, the breath/void/body-contraction-variety — thence the many person. He is the enjoyer, the bound; the enjoyment (bhoga) is the action-bliss two (the kriyā-jñāna powers) seen as pleasure and suffering.

(lines 11092) — the Lord's knowledge-action as the paśu's guṇas:** > In the own-member-form beings, of the Lord the knowledge and the action, which — with the māyā-third, > they alone are of the animal the being-ness (sattva), the rajas, the darkness (tamas). In the Lord, everywhere, the manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness are the knowledge-action powers; the māyā-power, opening the this-ness in the Sadāśiva-Īśa word, is the covering. In the own-form-un- cognition, in the beings, the knowledge and action are the pure-alone distinct-ness; with respect to the animal, the manifestation/un-manifestation are the sattva/rajas/tamas.

(lines 11112) — the power-ness not declared from the distinction:** > From the distinction-standing, of the power-possessor, the power-ness is not declared; of these > qualities, the instrument-effect-ness-transforming. The distinction-dealing is considered: the contracted consciousness-mere-nature is the person; his natural manifestation is not a power (by the connection with the other). The sattva-and-the-rest, standing by the distinction, are not power-declarable. The person, from the enjoyer-form, thinks them distinct; but in truth, even the earth-end ones, being power-form, are not thus.

(line ~11150) — the being-bliss-action of the Lord, the that-absence of the animal:** > The being-bliss-action of the Lord; the that-absence-even, she, of the animal — the two-own, that > rajas, the suffering, attached, the sattva-tamas-made. The Lord's being-ness (sattā) is the flashing, the agent-ness; the action-power is the pure reflexive-awareness; the bliss-power is the rest-form. Of the animal, the being-ness-bliss is the that-absence (the absence of the full being-bliss), two-own. The sattva (manifestation-pleasure), the tamas (the covering), and the rajas (the mixed, attached, suffering).

(line ~11190) — the non-conventional this-ness of the Lord:** > Who-even, of the non-conventional-this-ness-re-recollection-ground Lord — they, the mixed, and the > distinct, thus the varied-manifesting. In the Lord, even the appearances, mixed and distinct, are the innate (non-conventional) this-ness-re-recollection, the varied manifestation; in the Īśvara-state, the śūnya (the to-be-removed void) is the Rudra-presided, manifesting as the I-ness-negation.

(line 8271/11200) — the distinct-manifestation-meanings of the inner-self:** > They-though, the distinct-manifestation-meanings, the constructed, of the inner-self — with the > that-that-distinct-designations, in the memory-conjecture-and-the-rest range. The Īśvara's objects are the pure reflexive-awareness objects, all; but of the animal, they are the constructed (vikalpyāḥ), the distinct-manifestation, per-being, per-state, with the own-impression- following designations ("dear-this, enemy-this"); the inner-self (pratyagātman), the body-and-the-rest contracted, the "I"-being. The śūnya-pramātṛ, the infinite-regress, and its non-fault close the vimarśa's core.

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** The tattvasaṅgraha's middle section (kārikās 9–15) expounds the bond (bandha) and
its relation to the knower and the known. The central problem: the bound knower (paśu) creates his own
world — but how is this creation related to the Lord's creation? And what is the difference between the
bound and the liberated? Kārikās 9–15 answer: the paśu's creation is *asādhāraṇī* (un-common, private),
sustained by the Lord's creation (k9–10); the Lord's own creation is *sādhāraṇā* (common), and through
the abandonment of construction (vikalpahāna) one attains the Lord-ness (k11–12); the known is common,
but the liberated knows it with the own-self-non-difference (k13); in the supreme Śiva there is no
separate known at all (k14); and the fruit is the samyag jñāna-kriyā, the while-living-liberated (k15).
argument_steps: (lines 11600–11700) — the paśu's un-common creation:** > "This," indeed, of that, the un-common creation, the Lord-creation-dependent; she-even, with the > un-knowing-ness, in-the-existing-alone, with the Lord-power, with the that-self — The paśu's un-common (asādhāraṇī) creation is the Lord-creation-dependent (īśasṛṣṭyujīvinī) — it subsists on the back of the Lord's creation. It is per-knower, per-time, devoid of other-knower-state- following. The objection: "if the paśu creates, is it not common like the Lord's?" — No: the paśu's own power is un-known to him (being other-dependent), and only the Lord-ness awakens it. From the un-cognition alone comes the bound/liberated-ness. The māyā-power of the Lord — the word-mass body, the world-re-recollection-form — is the varṇadevatā-wheel, the eight-fold class (vargāṣṭaka), the ka-and-the-rest syllables; its movement (prāṇāpāna-swing) forbids firmness, and makes the "friend-this, enemy-this" constructions. The paśu's asādhāraṇī sṛṣṭi depends on the īśvara-created appearances (e.g. the "ten-tusked elephant"). The sūtra-meaning.

(lines 11700–11850) — the prāṇarūpā vikalpakriyā:** > With the own-rest-obstruction, with the moving, with the breath-form; with the construction-action, > the that-that-syllable-variety-form — The construction-action (vikalpakriyā), of the breath-form, is for the obstruction of the own rest. The māyāśakti (in the māyā-word, the kriyātmikā) binds the paśu (the Spa. 3.16). The kṣetrajña's creations are sabhittika (based, on the Lord's), not nirbhittika. The varṇadevatās (the ka-and-the-rest) are the infinite syllable-forms. Even the free constructions (the "king-I-stand") are, on inspection, parādhīnā (other-dependent). The māyā's three parts (tucchatābhāsa, vaiparītyābhāsa, nañartha) spread with the three stains.

(lines 11852–12068) — the sādhāraṇā aiśvarī sarga and the vikalpahāna:** > The common-alone, the-other, and-the-Lord's-creation, from-the-clear-manifestation; from-the- > construction-removal, from-the-one-pointedness, by-order, the-Lord-ness-word — The Lord's creation is clear-manifestation (spaṣṭāvabhāsana), hence un-constructed; it is sādhāraṇa or asādhāraṇa (the double-moon), both other-than the paśu's creation. When, by the abandonment of construction and the one-pointedness, the paśu attains the "I-this" Lord-ship-re-recollection, he destroys his animal-ness and shows the Lord-ness (the Vīrāvalī-Bhairava 113). Even the paśu's creation, if known with the Lord's power, becomes sādhāraṇa. In the dream, the constructions are clear or un-clear; the all-known-common-ness. The pratyayasṛṣṭi (the cognition-creation) is the kārmamalāpyāyikā; the kṣetrajñā's un-freedom (Spa. 3.14). The vikalpanirhrāsa (the thinning of construction) through the ekāgratā-practice leads to the param-Lord-word; the tattvārthasaṅgraha's non-repetition; the Vidyā-kalāśaktis; the svabhāvahetu and the pratyakṣa (the agnīndhana example).

(lines 12070–12109) — the viśvātman's maheśatā:** > All-mine-this-splendor, thus-of-the-knowing — of-the-world-self, of-the-constructions, in-the- > spread-even, the-mahā-Lord-ness — With the thinning of construction and the non-construction-assimilation, the own-cognition is the liberation (self-manifest). The "not another I" — the grāhyagrāhakaprakāśaghana param-eśvara is the "aham"; the constructions, fallen into the great re-recollection, become non-construction. The Pāradarśana ("even doubt is not doubted"); the Śivadṛṣṭi 1.38 (the sārvabhauma king playing the soldier); the prakṛtitvam-prāptān vikārān ākaroti; the ṛtudhāmā Āditya. The maheśvarataiva (the vṛtti, the pratyabhijñā).

(lines 12111–12140) — the known is common; the liberated knows it with the own-self:** > The-known-the-common, the-liberated-with-the-own-self-non-distinction-he-thinks; the-mahā-Lord-as, > the-bound-again-with-the-utter-distinction-endowed — The mukta, from the Sādākhya-word down to the embryo, knows the mātṛvarga as the "I-this," with the self-non-difference; the meya is common (mutually and from the knower-group un-distinguished), the ekarasābhedaviśrānti (the Śivadṛṣṭi 5.106, 7.91, 7.93). The baddha, in the reversal, is the ekaghanabhedaviśrānta. The tulyam (equal) is the kriyāviśeṣaṇa.

(lines 12142–12157) — in the supreme Śiva, no separate known:** > In-every-way-though-the-inner-dissolved-infinite-category-flood-filled; the-Śiva, the-consciousness- > bliss-mass, the-param-syllable-form — In the Sadāśiva-Īśa ground and the jīvanmukti, the known-order was examined; but in the parama-Śiva there is no known at all. The "sarvathā" (in every way) excludes; the "filled" (nirbhara) is the param-ness — the "I"-experience alone is filled; the ahaṃpratītir eva pūryate. The cidānandaghana is the filled "I"-experience; the paramākṣara is explained likewise.

(lines 12161–12263) — the fruit: the samyag jñāna-kriyā and the jīvanmukta:** > Thus-the-own-self-of-this, well-the-knowledge-action-two-thus; knowing-the-as-desired-beings, > seeing, he-knows-and-he-does-and — The fruit of the four-section teaching: knowing the own-self as the Lord-form, seeing the knowledge-action powers (not by the Kāpila/Kāṇāda views), one knows and does whatever one wishes — the jīvanmukta, who at the fall of the body is the param-eśvara. The māyā-word too is the citprakāśa (deśakālāspṛṣṭa); the sadāśiveśa-form; the Buddhists (the kṣaṇika, the virodhacintā, the paramāṇusaṅkoca) refuted; the niravabhāsā saṃvid; the ābhāsa-vimarśa stability (the śukti-rajata); the ekānekarūpatā; the idantāparāmarśa; the aikādhikaraṇya īśvaratā/śivatā; the paramaśivarūpāntarlīna īśvaratā (Spa. 1.2). The ||3|| colophon.

Proceed. The argument is understood: the paśu's creation is private, sustained by the Lord's (k9); the

argument_map.what_is_at_issue:
**The question:** This is the final vimarśa of the entire Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī. It is the
closing sum (samastanigamana) that draws together the whole teaching. Its theme: the transmission of the
teaching — from the guru, from the śāstra, and from the self (gurutaḥ, śāstrataḥ, svataḥ) — and the
recognition that is the fruit. It ends with the vivṛtikāra's own lineage-praise (17 ślokas), the final
stuti, and the two colophons that close the work.
argument_steps: **Maṅgala (lines 12265–12266):** "Bowing to the spread, the world that, from the un-surpassed form, in the order of bliss and the rest, emits the all-nectar-bearing, within and without…" **The threefold transmission (lines 12268–12307):** With the knowledge-action two-section-pair, and the essence-collection, the self-manifest essence, reason-augmented, was established; the "by-itself" (svataḥ) part was filled. The "from-the-śāstra" (śāstrataḥ) part is filled by the āgama-section. And the "from-the-guru" (gurutaḥ) part is the third, to be filled — for the śāstra-vision, too, must be brought to the proper-āgama-ness by the guru-lineage teaching. (The warning: "the book-studied knowledges, without the guru-order — practicing and teaching, they ripen long in hell; the censured enjoyers of the torment-king-of-kings; thence, teaching the guru-order-come — the param-Śiva.") The three verses (the ślokatraya) fill this: the first shows the lineage from the ādi-Śrīkaṇṭhanātha (the un-precedented, effort-less teaching); the second that the teaching, by the recognition-manifestation, animates even the real-as-un-real; the third that the worship of the prior gurus is necessary ("the to-be-celebrated guru-group, for the fame of the śāstra-meaning"). The lineage: Śrīkaṇṭhanātha → Durvāsa → Tryambakāditya (the Traiyambaka), the mānasa-sons.

(lines 12309–12383) — the new, well-fitted path:** > Thus is made manifest by me, this well-fitted, new path; by the great gurus it is spoken, in the > Śivadṛṣṭi-śāstra, as; placing the foot here, perceiving the world-creator-ness of the self, entering > the Śiva-ness-made continuously, he perfects. Since liberation is from the recognition alone, the yama/niyama-effort-yoga is useless here; the clear-means, effort-less, un-undertaken, great-fruit. The breath-control-yogas are artificial (kṛtrimā); the un-made has not the ṣoḍaśī-part. The "king-I-stand, enemy-by-me-killed" — the kingdom-imagination — is still other-dependent (parādhīnā). The māyāpade too is the citprakāśa (deśakālāspṛṣṭa); the jīvanmukta (the "jīvanneva mukta," the while-living-liberated); the dehapātād ekabhaviko mokṣa ("from the body-fall, the one-birth liberation"); the adbhutatama (the most wondrous).

(lines 12385–12405) — the kāntā/loka analogy:** > With-those-those-petitioned-favours, the-sought-to-by-the-slender-woman, standing-even-near; the > lover, like-the-world, the-un-known, not-for-enjoying, as; of-the-world, this-alone, thus, the > un-observed-quality, the-own-self-even, the-world-Lord; not-alone-for-the-own-splendor, this, that, > the-recognition-arisen — The lover, though standing near, sought by the slender woman, is not enjoyed while un-recognized; so the world-Lord, though always present, is not for his own splendor until the recognition arises. The pratyabhijñānamātra-ānandalābha vs. the pariśīlana-saṃbhogasahasra; the tattvedantayoḥ ekīkaraṇa = the īśvaratāhantayoḥ; the āśrayaucitya (the dṛṣṭānta/dārṣṭāntika ornament).

(lines 12407–12413) — the utpala-colophon:** > Of-the-people-for-the-effort-less-establishment, by-the-sun-rise-son (Uddayākarasūnu = Utpala); the > Lord-recognition, this, is-established — The recognition, established by Utpala for the people's effort-less establishment; the jananadharmā-siddhi (not caste/conduct); the sarvānugrāhakatva; the kṛtakṛtyatva (the father's fame-fruit). Then the vivṛtikāra's explanation: the susaṃvitti of the īśvaratā; the lāṭa/dvijatva/ vāgīśvarī; the antaḥprakṛti; the Karka-śāstra; the Tryambaka (tisro devyaḥ) and the dāsya-lakṣmī; the kheṭapālācārya (dvaita-prādhānya); the avidyā (anirvācya); the brahmavāda (not ekāntavāda); the "cittamātram idaṃ" (the Buddhist) and the vivaraṇakāra-vipratāraṇa; the prathāto'khilagrahaṇa (all that is prathamāna = the parama-śiva's prathā); the paryantopāsanīya parama-śiva. **The vivṛtikāra's 17 ślokas (lines 12453–12517) — the author-lineage praise:** The vaṃśa (1–15) praises the lineage — Varāha-gupta (Cukhulaka, Bhūtirāja's father), Bhūtirāja, Haṭitalakṣmaṇagupta (the śāstra-maker, Abhinava's guru), the Tryambaka-śaktitraya, the māṇikyācala/Candrakīrti, the vimarśa-method of the Lord-recognition (9), the varṇanikā (10), the vāsanācakravāla (11), the arkameka (12), the ātmāvaraṇa/ātmaprakaṭana (14), and the navatitama-vatsara (year 90, Mārgaśīrṣa) colophon (15). The final stuti (16–17: the parama-śiva-stuti, "īśvarapratyabhijñā … vimarśād īśvareṇa … tmavimarśodyoginīṃ kriyāt"). **The ||4|| and samāptā colophons (lines 12528–12539):** "Thus, in the mahā-māheśvara-Śrīmad-ācārya-Abhinavagupta-composed, in the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī, the all-conclusion, the fourth vimarśa || 4 ||." "Completed, and, this, the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī; the composition of the Śrī-Tri-nayana-foot-meditation- obtained-fame Abhinavagupta-foots." — the END of the whole IPVV.
